source_paragraphs: HIGH above the city, on a tall column, stood the statue of the Happy Prince.  He was gilded all over with thin leaves of fine gold, for eyes he had two bright sapphires, and a large red ruby glowed on his sword-hilt.

He was very much admired indeed.  “He is as beautiful as a weathercock,” remarked one of the Town Councillors who wished to gain a reputation for having artistic tastes; “only not quite so useful,” he added, fearing lest people should think him unpractical, which he really was not.
“Why can’t you be like the Happy Prince?” asked a sensible mother of her little boy who was crying for the moon.  “The Happy Prince never dreams of crying for anything.”
“I am glad there is some one in the world who is quite happy,” muttered a disappointed man as he gazed at the wonderful statue.
“He looks just like an angel,” said the Charity Children as they came out of the cathedral in their bright scarlet cloaks and their clean white pinafores.
“How do you know?” said the Mathematical Master, “you have never seen one.”
“Ah! but we have, in our dreams,” answered the children; and the Mathematical Master frowned and looked very severe, for he did not approve of children dreaming.

One night there flew over the city a little Swallow.  His friends had gone away to Egypt six weeks before, but he had stayed behind, for he was in love with the most beautiful Reed.  He had met her early in the spring as he was flying down the river after a big yellow moth, and had been so attracted by her slender waist that he had stopped to talk to her.

“Shall I love you?” said the Swallow, who liked to come to the point at once, and the Reed made him a low bow.  So he flew round and round her, touching the water with his wings, and making silver ripples.  This was his courtship, and it lasted all through the summer.

“It is a ridiculous attachment,” twittered the other Swallows; “she has no money, and far too many relations”; and indeed the river was quite full of Reeds.  Then, when the autumn came they all flew away.

After they had gone he felt lonely, and began to tire of his lady-love. “She has no conversation,” he said, “and I am afraid that she is a coquette, for she is always flirting with the wind.”  And certainly, whenever the wind blew, the Reed made the most graceful curtseys.  “I admit that she is domestic,” he continued, “but I love travelling, and my wife, consequently, should love travelling also.”
“Will you come away with me?” he said finally to her; but the Reed shook her head, she was so attached to her home.
“You have been trifling with me,” he cried.  “I am off to the Pyramids. Good-bye!” and he flew away.
All day long he flew, and at night-time he arrived at the city.  “Where shall I put up?” he said; “I hope the town has made preparations.”
Then he saw the statue on the tall column.
“I will put up there,” he cried; “it is a fine position, with plenty of fresh air.”  So he alighted just between the feet of the Happy Prince.

“I have a golden bedroom,” he said softly to himself as he looked round, and he prepared to go to sleep; but just as he was putting his head under his wing a large drop of water fell on him.  “What a curious thing!” he cried; “there is not a single cloud in the sky, the stars are quite clear and bright, and yet it is raining.  The climate in the north of Europe is really dreadful.  The Reed used to like the rain, but that was merely her selfishness.”
Then another drop fell.
“What is the use of a statue if it cannot keep the rain off?” he said; “I must look for a good chimney-pot,” and he determined to fly away.
But before he had opened his wings, a third drop fell, and he looked up, and saw—Ah! what did he see?
The eyes of the Happy Prince were filled with tears, and tears were running down his golden cheeks.  His face was so beautiful in the moonlight that the little Swallow was filled with pity.
“Who are you?” he said.
“I am the Happy Prince.”
“Why are you weeping then?” asked the Swallow; “you have quite drenched me.”

“When I was alive and had a human heart,” answered the statue, “I did not know what tears were, for I lived in the Palace of Sans-Souci, where sorrow is not allowed to enter.  In the daytime I played with my companions in the garden, and in the evening I led the dance in the Great Hall.  Round the garden ran a very lofty wall, but I never cared to ask what lay beyond it, everything about me was so beautiful.  My courtiers called me the Happy Prince, and happy indeed I was, if pleasure be happiness.  So I lived, and so I died.  And now that I am dead they have set me up here so high that I can see all the ugliness and all the misery of my city, and though my heart is made of lead yet I cannot chose but weep.”
“What! is he not solid gold?” said the Swallow to himself.  He was too polite to make any personal remarks out loud.

“Far away,” continued the statue in a low musical voice, “far away in a little street there is a poor house.  One of the windows is open, and through it I can see a woman seated at a table.  Her face is thin and worn, and she has coarse, red hands, all pricked by the needle, for she is a seamstress.  She is embroidering passion-flowers on a satin gown for the loveliest of the Queen’s maids-of-honour to wear at the next Court-ball.  In a bed in the corner of the room her little boy is lying ill.  He has a fever, and is asking for oranges.  His mother has nothing to give him but river water, so he is crying.  Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow, will you not bring her the ruby out of my sword-hilt?  My feet are fastened to this pedestal and I cannot move.”

“I am waited for in Egypt,” said the Swallow.  “My friends are flying up and down the Nile, and talking to the large lotus-flowers.  Soon they will go to sleep in the tomb of the great King.  The King is there himself in his painted coffin.  He is wrapped in yellow linen, and embalmed with spices.  Round his neck is a chain of pale green jade, and his hands are like withered leaves.”
“Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “will you not stay with me for one night, and be my messenger?  The boy is so thirsty, and the mother so sad.”

“I don’t think I like boys,” answered the Swallow.  “Last summer, when I was staying on the river, there were two rude boys, the miller’s sons, who were always throwing stones at me.  They never hit me, of course; we swallows fly far too well for that, and besides, I come of a family famous for its agility; but still, it was a mark of disrespect.”
But the Happy Prince looked so sad that the little Swallow was sorry. “It is very cold here,” he said; “but I will stay with you for one night, and be your messenger.”
“Thank you, little Swallow,” said the Prince.
So the Swallow picked out the great ruby from the Prince’s sword, and flew away with it in his beak over the roofs of the town.

He passed by the cathedral tower, where the white marble angels were sculptured.  He passed by the palace and heard the sound of dancing.  A beautiful girl came out on the balcony with her lover.  “How wonderful the stars are,” he said to her, “and how wonderful is the power of love!”
“I hope my dress will be ready in time for the State-ball,” she answered; “I have ordered passion-flowers to be embroidered on it; but the seamstresses are so lazy.”

He passed over the river, and saw the lanterns hanging to the masts of the ships.  He passed over the Ghetto, and saw the old Jews bargaining with each other, and weighing out money in copper scales.  At last he came to the poor house and looked in.  The boy was tossing feverishly on his bed, and the mother had fallen asleep, she was so tired.  In he hopped, and laid the great ruby on the table beside the woman’s thimble. Then he flew gently round the bed, fanning the boy’s forehead with his wings.  “How cool I feel,” said the boy, “I must be getting better”; and he sank into a delicious slumber.
Then the Swallow flew back to the Happy Prince, and told him what he had done.  “It is curious,” he remarked, “but I feel quite warm now, although it is so cold.”
“That is because you have done a good action,” said the Prince.  And the little Swallow began to think, and then he fell asleep.  Thinking always made him sleepy.

When day broke he flew down to the river and had a bath.  “What a remarkable phenomenon,” said the Professor of Ornithology as he was passing over the bridge.  “A swallow in winter!”  And he wrote a long letter about it to the local newspaper.  Every one quoted it, it was full of so many words that they could not understand.

“To-night I go to Egypt,” said the Swallow, and he was in high spirits at the prospect.  He visited all the public monuments, and sat a long time on top of the church steeple.  Wherever he went the Sparrows chirruped, and said to each other, “What a distinguished stranger!” so he enjoyed himself very much.
When the moon rose he flew back to the Happy Prince.  “Have you any commissions for Egypt?” he cried; “I am just starting.”
“Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “will you not stay with me one night longer?”

“I am waited for in Egypt,” answered the Swallow.  “To-morrow my friends will fly up to the Second Cataract.  The river-horse couches there among the bulrushes, and on a great granite throne sits the God Memnon.  All night long he watches the stars, and when the morning star shines he utters one cry of joy, and then he is silent.  At noon the yellow lions come down to the water’s edge to drink.  They have eyes like green beryls, and their roar is louder than the roar of the cataract.”

“Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “far away across the city I see a young man in a garret.  He is leaning over a desk covered with papers, and in a tumbler by his side there is a bunch of withered violets.  His hair is brown and crisp, and his lips are red as a pomegranate, and he has large and dreamy eyes.  He is trying to finish a play for the Director of the Theatre, but he is too cold to write any more.  There is no fire in the grate, and hunger has made him faint.”
“I will wait with you one night longer,” said the Swallow, who really had a good heart.  “Shall I take him another ruby?”

“Alas!  I have no ruby now,” said the Prince; “my eyes are all that I have left.  They are made of rare sapphires, which were brought out of India a thousand years ago.  Pluck out one of them and take it to him. He will sell it to the jeweller, and buy food and firewood, and finish his play.”
“Dear Prince,” said the Swallow, “I cannot do that”; and he began to weep.
“Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “do as I command you.”

So the Swallow plucked out the Prince’s eye, and flew away to the student’s garret.  It was easy enough to get in, as there was a hole in the roof.  Through this he darted, and came into the room.  The young man had his head buried in his hands, so he did not hear the flutter of the bird’s wings, and when he looked up he found the beautiful sapphire lying on the withered violets.
“I am beginning to be appreciated,” he cried; “this is from some great admirer.  Now I can finish my play,” and he looked quite happy.

The next day the Swallow flew down to the harbour.  He sat on the mast of a large vessel and watched the sailors hauling big chests out of the hold with ropes.  “Heave a-hoy!” they shouted as each chest came up.  “I am going to Egypt”! cried the Swallow, but nobody minded, and when the moon rose he flew back to the Happy Prince.
“I am come to bid you good-bye,” he cried.
“Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “will you not stay with me one night longer?”

“It is winter,” answered the Swallow, “and the chill snow will soon be here.  In Egypt the sun is warm on the green palm-trees, and the crocodiles lie in the mud and look lazily about them.  My companions are building a nest in the Temple of Baalbec, and the pink and white doves are watching them, and cooing to each other.  Dear Prince, I must leave you, but I will never forget you, and next spring I will bring you back two beautiful jewels in place of those you have given away.  The ruby shall be redder than a red rose, and the sapphire shall be as blue as the great sea.”

“In the square below,” said the Happy Prince, “there stands a little match-girl.  She has let her matches fall in the gutter, and they are all spoiled.  Her father will beat her if she does not bring home some money, and she is crying.  She has no shoes or stockings, and her little head is bare.  Pluck out my other eye, and give it to her, and her father will not beat her.”
“I will stay with you one night longer,” said the Swallow, “but I cannot pluck out your eye.  You would be quite blind then.”
“Swallow, Swallow, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “do as I command you.”

So he plucked out the Prince’s other eye, and darted down with it.  He swooped past the match-girl, and slipped the jewel into the palm of her hand.  “What a lovely bit of glass,” cried the little girl; and she ran home, laughing.
Then the Swallow came back to the Prince.  “You are blind now,” he said, “so I will stay with you always.”
“No, little Swallow,” said the poor Prince, “you must go away to Egypt.”
“I will stay with you always,” said the Swallow, and he slept at the Prince’s feet.

All the next day he sat on the Prince’s shoulder, and told him stories of what he had seen in strange lands.  He told him of the red ibises, who stand in long rows on the banks of the Nile, and catch gold-fish in their beaks; of the Sphinx, who is as old as the world itself, and lives in the desert, and knows everything; of the merchants, who walk slowly by the side of their camels, and carry amber beads in their hands; of the King of the Mountains of the Moon, who is as black as ebony, and worships a large crystal; of the great green snake that sleeps in a palm-tree, and has twenty priests to feed it with honey-cakes; and of the pygmies who sail over a big lake on large flat leaves, and are always at war with the butterflies.

“Dear little Swallow,” said the Prince, “you tell me of marvellous things, but more marvellous than anything is the suffering of men and of women.  There is no Mystery so great as Misery.  Fly over my city, little Swallow, and tell me what you see there.”

So the Swallow flew over the great city, and saw the rich making merry in their beautiful houses, while the beggars were sitting at the gates.  He flew into dark lanes, and saw the white faces of starving children looking out listlessly at the black streets.  Under the archway of a bridge two little boys were lying in one another’s arms to try and keep themselves warm.  “How hungry we are!” they said.  “You must not lie here,” shouted the Watchman, and they wandered out into the rain.
Then he flew back and told the Prince what he had seen.
“I am covered with fine gold,” said the Prince, “you must take it off, leaf by leaf, and give it to my poor; the living always think that gold can make them happy.”

Leaf after leaf of the fine gold the Swallow picked off, till the Happy Prince looked quite dull and grey.  Leaf after leaf of the fine gold he brought to the poor, and the children’s faces grew rosier, and they laughed and played games in the street.  “We have bread now!” they cried.

Then the snow came, and after the snow came the frost.  The streets looked as if they were made of silver, they were so bright and glistening; long icicles like crystal daggers hung down from the eaves of the houses, everybody went about in furs, and the little boys wore scarlet caps and skated on the ice.

The poor little Swallow grew colder and colder, but he would not leave the Prince, he loved him too well.  He picked up crumbs outside the baker’s door when the baker was not looking and tried to keep himself warm by flapping his wings.
But at last he knew that he was going to die.  He had just strength to fly up to the Prince’s shoulder once more.  “Good-bye, dear Prince!” he murmured, “will you let me kiss your hand?”
“I am glad that you are going to Egypt at last, little Swallow,” said the Prince, “you have stayed too long here; but you must kiss me on the lips, for I love you.”
“It is not to Egypt that I am going,” said the Swallow.  “I am going to the House of Death.  Death is the brother of Sleep, is he not?”
And he kissed the Happy Prince on the lips, and fell down dead at his feet.
At that moment a curious crack sounded inside the statue, as if something had broken.  The fact is that the leaden heart had snapped right in two. It certainly was a dreadfully hard frost.

Early the next morning the Mayor was walking in the square below in company with the Town Councillors.  As they passed the column he looked up at the statue: “Dear me! how shabby the Happy Prince looks!” he said.
“How shabby indeed!” cried the Town Councillors, who always agreed with the Mayor; and they went up to look at it.
“The ruby has fallen out of his sword, his eyes are gone, and he is golden no longer,” said the Mayor in fact, “he is little better than a beggar!”
“Little better than a beggar,” said the Town Councillors.

“And here is actually a dead bird at his feet!” continued the Mayor.  “We must really issue a proclamation that birds are not to be allowed to die here.”  And the Town Clerk made a note of the suggestion.
So they pulled down the statue of the Happy Prince.  “As he is no longer beautiful he is no longer useful,” said the Art Professor at the University.

Then they melted the statue in a furnace, and the Mayor held a meeting of the Corporation to decide what was to be done with the metal.  “We must have another statue, of course,” he said, “and it shall be a statue of myself.”
“Of myself,” said each of the Town Councillors, and they quarrelled. When I last heard of them they were quarrelling still.

“What a strange thing!” said the overseer of the workmen at the foundry. “This broken lead heart will not melt in the furnace.  We must throw it away.”  So they threw it on a dust-heap where the dead Swallow was also lying.
“Bring me the two most precious things in the city,” said God to one of His Angels; and the Angel brought Him the leaden heart and the dead bird.
“You have rightly chosen,” said God, “for in my garden of Paradise this little bird shall sing for evermore, and in my city of gold the Happy Prince shall praise me.”
translated_paragraphs: 高高的石柱上，快乐王子的雕像耸立在整座城上方。他浑身贴满薄薄的足金箔，两颗明亮的蓝宝石做了他的眼睛。剑柄上，一颗硕大的红宝石闪着光。
人们着实很仰慕他。“他跟风向标上的公鸡一样漂亮，”一位市议员说。这位议员很想得个懂艺术的好名声。“只是没那么管用。”他怕别人说他不讲实际。他这个人确实很讲实际。
“你为什么不能学学快乐王子？”一个懂道理的妈妈问她的小儿子。孩子哭着要月亮。“快乐王子才不会为要什么东西哭鼻子。”
“幸好这世上总还有一个快快乐乐的人。”一个事事不如意的人望着那奇妙的塑像，低声说。
“他多像天使呀！”慈善学校的孩子们说。他们正从大教堂出来，身披鲜红的斗篷，胸前是雪白干净的围裙。
“你们怎么知道？你们又没见过天使。”数学老师说。
“啊，可我们见过呀，在梦里！”孩子们说。数学老师皱起眉头，脸色严厉了起来。他不赞成小孩做梦。
一天夜里，一只小燕子飞过这座城。他的朋友们六个星期前就去埃及了，他却留了下来，因为他爱上了一棵最美的芦苇。他们在初春相遇，那时他正顺着河追一只黄色的大飞蛾。芦苇纤细的腰身迷住了他，他便停下来同她讲话。
“我来爱你，好吗？”燕子说。他喜欢有话直说。芦苇深深地向他弯了弯腰。于是他便绕着她一圈圈地飞，翅尖掠过水面，划出银色的波纹。他就是这样求爱的，整整持续了一个夏天。
“这热恋也太可笑了，”别的燕子叽叽喳喳地说，“她一个钱也没有，亲戚倒多得很。”的确，满河都是芦苇。等秋天一来，他们就全飞走了。
他们走后，小燕子觉得孤单，对他的意中人也有些厌倦了。“她连话也不说。我看她恐怕还爱卖弄风情呢，她老跟风调情。”的确，每次风一吹，芦苇就姿态优美地屈膝行礼。“我承认她很恋家，”他又说，“可是我爱旅行，我未来的妻子也该爱旅行才对。”
“你愿意跟我走吗？”他终于问。芦苇摇了摇头。她跟自己的家实在难舍难分。“你一直在逗我玩！”他叫道，“我上金字塔去啦。再见！”说完就飞走了。
他飞了一整天，夜里才到了这座城。“住哪儿好呢？”他说，“希望城里早有安排。”这时他看见了高柱上的雕像。“就住那儿吧！位置好极了，新鲜空气管够。”他就在快乐王子的两脚之间落下。
“我有一间黄金卧室呢。”他朝四下望望，小声说，准备睡觉。正要把头藏进翅膀底下，啪嗒，一大滴水落到他身上。“这可怪了！天上一片云都没有，星星又清楚又明亮，倒下起雨来。北欧的天气实在太坏了。芦苇从前还喜欢雨呢，可那是因为她只顾自己。”
又落下一滴。“连雨都遮不住，要雕像有什么用？我得找一根好烟囱。”他说着就打算飞走。不等他张开翅膀，第三滴也落了下来。他抬起头。啊！你猜他看见了什么？
快乐王子的两眼噙满了泪水。眼泪顺着他金色的面颊淌下来。月光里，他的脸那样美，小燕子心里满是怜惜。
“你是谁？”他问。“我是快乐王子。”“那么你为什么哭呢？你把我淋得浑身都湿透了。”

“我活着，还有一颗人心的时候，”雕像说，“一点也不知道眼泪是什么。我住在无忧宫，忧愁是不准进去的。白天我和伙伴们在花园里玩，夜里在大厅里领舞。园子四面围着很高的墙，我从没想问墙外有什么，我身边的一切已经够美了。大臣们都叫我快乐王子。如果享乐就是快乐，我的确十分快乐。我就这样活，也就这样死。如今我死了，他们把我放在这么高的地方，城里一切丑陋和苦难，我都看得一清二楚。我的心虽是铅做的，还是忍不住要哭。”
“怎么，他不是纯金铸的？”小燕子在心里嘀咕。他很有礼貌，不肯当面议论人家的身体。

“远远的，”雕像接着说，声音低低的，像音乐，“远远的一条小街上，有间穷人家的屋子。一扇窗开着，我看见一个妇人坐在桌边。她的脸消瘦又憔悴，两只手又红又粗，满是针扎的印子，因为她靠针线过活。她正在一件缎子礼服上绣西番莲，好让王后身边最美的侍女穿去参加下一场宫廷舞会。屋角的床上，躺着她生病的小儿子。他正在发烧，想吃橙子。母亲除了河水，什么也给不了，于是他哭起来。燕子，燕子，小燕子，你肯从我剑柄上取下红宝石，送去给她吗？我的双脚固定在石座上，动也动不了。”
“埃及还有朋友等我呢，”小燕子说，“他们正沿着尼罗河来回飞，跟河里的大莲花谈天。再过不久，他们就要到古代大王的坟墓里睡觉。大王自己也在那里，躺在彩绘的棺材中。黄色亚麻布裹着他，他的身体用香料保存。他脖子上挂着淡绿色的玉石项链，两只手像枯萎的树叶。”
“燕子，燕子，小燕子，”王子说，“你肯陪我一夜，替我做个信使吗？那孩子渴得很，母亲又那么难过。”
“我想我不大喜欢男孩子，”小燕子说，“去年夏天我住在河边，有两个没礼貌的男孩，磨坊主的儿子，老捡石头朝我扔来。他们当然一次也没打中。我们燕子飞得好极了，更何况我家祖祖辈辈都以身手敏捷出名。可不管怎么说，那也太没礼貌了。”
快乐王子脸上的忧伤叫小燕子心软了。“这儿很冷，”他说，“不过，我愿意陪你一夜，给你当信使。”“谢谢你，小燕子。”王子说。
于是燕子从剑柄上啄下大红宝石，衔着它飞过城里的屋顶。他飞过大教堂的塔，塔上刻着白色大理石天使。他飞过王宫，听见里面的舞乐。一个美丽姑娘同她的情人上了阳台。“星星多么奇妙，”情人说，“爱的力量又是多么奇妙！”
“我只盼我的礼服赶得上宫廷舞会，”她答道，“我吩咐在上面绣西番莲的，可那些女裁缝太懒了。”
他飞过河，看见船桅上挂着灯笼。他飞过犹太人居住的街区，看见几位老人正互相讲价，用铜天平称钱币。末了他来到那所穷屋，往里面瞧。发烧的孩子在床上翻来覆去，母亲太累，已经睡着了。他蹦进去，把那颗大红宝石轻轻放在桌上，就在她缝衣用的顶针旁。他轻轻绕着床飞，用翅膀给男孩的额头扇风。“多凉快呀，”男孩说，“我的病一定在好转。”说罢就舒舒服服地睡着了。
燕子飞回王子身边，讲了他做的事。“真奇怪，”他补了一句，“天气这么冷，我身上倒暖和起来了。”“因为你刚做了一件好事。”王子说。小燕子想了想，就睡着了。一动脑筋他就犯困。
天一亮，他便飞到河里洗澡。一位鸟类学教授正走过桥。“何等罕见的现象！冬天里竟有燕子！”他为这件事给当地报纸写了一封长信，人人都引用它，因为里头大家不认得的词实在太多了。
“今夜我就去埃及。”燕子想到这件事，高兴得很。他参观了城里所有的纪念碑，在教堂尖顶上坐了很久。每到一处，麻雀们都叽叽啾啾地议论：“多气派的一位贵客！”这一天他过得真愉快。
月亮升起来，他飞回快乐王子身边。“有什么事要我捎到埃及去吗？我就动身。”
“燕子，燕子，小燕子，你肯再陪我一夜吗？”“埃及还有朋友等我，”小燕子答道，“明天他们要飞到尼罗河第二瀑布去。那里的灯心草丛中躺着河马，巨大的花岗岩王座上坐着门农神像。他整夜望着星星，等晨星发亮，他欢喜地叫一声，然后就安静了。到了正午，黄狮子们走到水边来喝水。它们的眼睛像绿色的宝石，吼声盖过瀑布的轰鸣。”
“燕子，燕子，小燕子，”王子说，“在城的另一端，我看见一间小阁楼。里面有个年轻人，伏在一张铺满纸的写字桌上。他身旁的玻璃杯里，插着一束枯萎的紫罗兰。他的头发棕褐，卷卷的，嘴唇红得像石榴，两只大眼睛像是常在做梦。他想给剧院经理写完一个剧本，却冷得再也写不下去。炉膛里没有火，他也饿得头昏了。”
“我就再陪你一夜吧，”小燕子说。他心地着实善良。“要我再送他一颗红宝石吗？”
“唉，红宝石已经没有了。只剩下我这双眼睛。它们是稀有的蓝宝石，一千年前从印度运来。把其中一颗啄下来送给他吧。他可以卖给珠宝商，买到吃的和柴火，把戏写完。”
“亲爱的王子，这我做不到。”燕子哭了起来。“燕子，燕子，小燕子，照我的吩咐去做吧。”
于是他啄下王子的一颗眼珠，飞到了那位年轻学生住的阁楼。进去倒不难，屋顶恰好有个洞。他一头钻进屋里。年轻人把脸埋在两手间，没听见翅膀扑动的声音。一抬头，忽然看见一颗美丽的蓝宝石卧在枯紫罗兰上。
“总算有人开始赏识我啦！”他喊道，“这一定是一位仰慕我的人送的。现在，我能把剧本写完了。”他的脸上现出了快活的神情。
第二天，小燕子飞去港口，停在一艘大船的桅杆上，看水手用绳索从货舱往上吊大箱子。每吊起一箱，水手们就喊一声：“嘿哟，起！”“我要去埃及啦！”燕子大叫，谁也没在意。到了月亮升起，他又飞回快乐王子身边。
“我来跟你告别。”他喊。“燕子，燕子，小燕子，你肯再多陪我一个晚上吗？”
“已经是冬天了，”燕子回答，“冰冷的雪很快就到。埃及的阳光暖暖地照着绿棕榈，鳄鱼趴在泥里，懒洋洋地张望。我的伙伴们在巴勒贝克神殿筑巢，粉白色的鸽子一面看，一面对着彼此咕咕叫。亲爱的王子，我必须走了。可我绝不会忘记你。明年春天我会带回两颗美丽的宝石，补上你送掉的。红宝石会比红玫瑰还红，蓝宝石会像大海一样蓝。”
“下边的广场上，站着一个卖火柴的小女孩，”快乐王子说，“她把火柴掉进水沟，火柴全坏了。要是带不回几个钱，她父亲会打她的。她哭了，脚上没有鞋袜，小脑袋也光着。啄下我另一只眼睛送给她吧，这样她父亲就不会打她了。”
“我愿意再陪你一夜，”燕子说，“可是我不能啄下你的眼睛。那你就什么都看不见了。”“燕子，燕子，小燕子，照我的吩咐去做吧。”
于是他啄下王子的另一只眼珠，衔着往下飞。他从小女孩身边一掠而过，悄悄把宝石放进她的手心。“多漂亮的一块玻璃呀！”小女孩叫着，笑着跑回家去了。
燕子回到王子身旁。“你现在看不见了，我就一直陪着你。”“不，小燕子，”可怜的王子说，“你该去埃及了。”“我会一直陪着你。”燕子就在王子的脚边睡了。
第二天，他整天坐在王子肩上，讲自己在远方看见的事。他讲排成长列的红鹮站在尼罗河岸，用喙捉起金鱼。讲那尊住在沙漠里、和世界同龄、无所不知的狮身人面像。讲手里拈着琥珀珠子，在骆驼身旁慢慢走的商人。讲月亮山国的国王，皮肤黑如乌木，敬奉一块硕大的水晶。讲睡在棕榈树上的大绿蛇，有二十个祭司专门用蜜饼喂它。还讲矮人驾着平阔的叶子横渡大湖，老是跟蝴蝶打仗。
“亲爱的小燕子，”王子说，“你讲的都是不可思议的事。可世上最不可思议的，是人们受的那些苦。再大的谜也大不过苦难。飞过我的城吧，小燕子，回来告诉我你看见了些什么。”
小燕子飞过整座大城。他看见富人在华美的屋子里寻欢作乐，乞丐就坐在他们大门口。他飞进幽暗的小巷，看见挨饿的孩子们探出苍白的脸，没精打采地望着漆黑的街道。桥洞里两个小男孩躺着，抱在一起取暖。“我们好饿呀！”他们说。“不准躺在这里！”巡夜人喊。两个孩子只好又走进雨中。
燕子把这些见闻讲给王子听。“我身上贴着足金的金箔，”王子说，“你把它们一片一片揭下来，送给我的穷人。活着的人总觉得，金子能让他们快乐。”
一片又一片，小燕子啄下金箔，直到快乐王子浑身暗淡发灰。一片又一片，他把金箔送给穷人。孩子们的脸色红润起来。他们笑着在街上做游戏。“我们有面包吃啦！”他们喊。
后来，下了雪，接着又结了霜。街道明晃晃的，好像是用银子做的。长冰柱像水晶匕首，从家家户户的屋檐底下倒悬下来。人们裹着皮衣出门，小男孩戴着鲜红的帽子在冰上滑冰。
可怜的小燕子越来越冷，却怎么也不肯离开王子。他太爱他了。他趁面包师傅没看见，到店门口捡些面包屑吃，又拍打着翅膀，尽力让自己暖和一点。
到最后，他知道自己快要死了。他拼尽所剩的一点力气，再一次飞上王子的肩头。“再见，亲爱的王子，”他低声说，“让我吻一下你的手，好吗？”
“我很高兴，你终于要去埃及了，小燕子，”王子说，“你在这儿待得太久。可是你该吻我的嘴唇，因为我爱你。”
“我要去的地方不叫埃及，”燕子说，“我要去的是死亡的家。死亡和睡眠，原是一对兄弟，对吗？”
他在快乐王子的唇上轻轻一吻，跌落在他脚边，死了。就在这时，雕像里面传出奇怪的一响，像有什么东西裂开了。原来，那颗铅做的心从中间断成了两半。那天晚上的霜冻也确实厉害。
第二天清早，市长和市议员们一道在广场上散步。经过石柱时，市长抬头望了一眼雕像。“哎呀！快乐王子看上去怎么这样寒碜！”“真寒碜哪！”市议员们喊。市长说什么，他们总是赞成的。于是大家就走近去细看。
“剑上的红宝石脱落了，眼睛也没了，浑身连金色都褪了，”市长说，“简直比乞丐好不了多少！”“比乞丐好不了多少！”市议员们说。
“瞧，他脚下居然还有一只死鸟！”市长继续说，“我们真该发一道公告，禁止鸟儿死在这里。”市书记官把这条意见记下了。
于是，他们推倒了快乐王子的雕像。“既然不再美了，也就没有用了。”大学里的艺术教授说。雕像被扔进炉子熔化，市长召集市政会议，讨论该怎么使用那些金属。“我们当然得再铸一座雕像，”他说，“就铸我的像吧。”
“铸我的像。”每一个市议员都这样说，于是他们吵了起来。据我最后听到的消息，他们还在吵呢。
“怪事！”铸造厂的工头说，“这颗碎铅心，在炉子里居然化不开。得把它扔掉。”他们便把铅心扔在垃圾堆上，那只死去的小燕子也躺在那里。
“把这座城里最珍贵的两样东西带给我。”上帝对一位天使说。天使便把那颗铅心和那只死去的鸟带到他面前。
“你选对了，”上帝说，“在我的乐园里，这只小鸟将永远歌唱。在我的黄金之城，快乐王子将向我献上赞歌。”

source_paragraphs: “SHE said that she would dance with me if I brought her red roses,” cried the young Student; “but in all my garden there is no red rose.”
From her nest in the holm-oak tree the Nightingale heard him, and she looked out through the leaves, and wondered.

“No red rose in all my garden!” he cried, and his beautiful eyes filled with tears.  “Ah, on what little things does happiness depend!  I have read all that the wise men have written, and all the secrets of philosophy are mine, yet for want of a red rose is my life made wretched.”

“Here at last is a true lover,” said the Nightingale.  “Night after night have I sung of him, though I knew him not: night after night have I told his story to the stars, and now I see him.  His hair is dark as the hyacinth-blossom, and his lips are red as the rose of his desire; but passion has made his face like pale ivory, and sorrow has set her seal upon his brow.”

“The Prince gives a ball to-morrow night,” murmured the young Student, “and my love will be of the company.  If I bring her a red rose she will dance with me till dawn.  If I bring her a red rose, I shall hold her in my arms, and she will lean her head upon my shoulder, and her hand will be clasped in mine.  But there is no red rose in my garden, so I shall sit lonely, and she will pass me by.  She will have no heed of me, and my heart will break.”

“Here indeed is the true lover,” said the Nightingale.  “What I sing of, he suffers—what is joy to me, to him is pain.  Surely Love is a wonderful thing.  It is more precious than emeralds, and dearer than fine opals. Pearls and pomegranates cannot buy it, nor is it set forth in the marketplace.  It may not be purchased of the merchants, nor can it be weighed out in the balance for gold.”

“The musicians will sit in their gallery,” said the young Student, “and play upon their stringed instruments, and my love will dance to the sound of the harp and the violin.  She will dance so lightly that her feet will not touch the floor, and the courtiers in their gay dresses will throng round her.  But with me she will not dance, for I have no red rose to give her”; and he flung himself down on the grass, and buried his face in his hands, and wept.
“Why is he weeping?” asked a little Green Lizard, as he ran past him with his tail in the air.
“Why, indeed?” said a Butterfly, who was fluttering about after a sunbeam.
“Why, indeed?” whispered a Daisy to his neighbour, in a soft, low voice.
“He is weeping for a red rose,” said the Nightingale.
“For a red rose?” they cried; “how very ridiculous!” and the little Lizard, who was something of a cynic, laughed outright.
But the Nightingale understood the secret of the Student’s sorrow, and she sat silent in the oak-tree, and thought about the mystery of Love.
Suddenly she spread her brown wings for flight, and soared into the air. She passed through the grove like a shadow, and like a shadow she sailed across the garden.
In the centre of the grass-plot was standing a beautiful Rose-tree, and when she saw it she flew over to it, and lit upon a spray.
“Give me a red rose,” she cried, “and I will sing you my sweetest song.”
But the Tree shook its head.

“My roses are white,” it answered; “as white as the foam of the sea, and whiter than the snow upon the mountain.  But go to my brother who grows round the old sun-dial, and perhaps he will give you what you want.”
So the Nightingale flew over to the Rose-tree that was growing round the old sun-dial.
“Give me a red rose,” she cried, “and I will sing you my sweetest song.”
But the Tree shook its head.

“My roses are yellow,” it answered; “as yellow as the hair of the mermaiden who sits upon an amber throne, and yellower than the daffodil that blooms in the meadow before the mower comes with his scythe.  But go to my brother who grows beneath the Student’s window, and perhaps he will give you what you want.”
So the Nightingale flew over to the Rose-tree that was growing beneath the Student’s window.
“Give me a red rose,” she cried, “and I will sing you my sweetest song.”
But the Tree shook its head.

“My roses are red,” it answered, “as red as the feet of the dove, and redder than the great fans of coral that wave and wave in the ocean-cavern.  But the winter has chilled my veins, and the frost has nipped my buds, and the storm has broken my branches, and I shall have no roses at all this year.”
“One red rose is all I want,” cried the Nightingale, “only one red rose! Is there no way by which I can get it?”
“There is a way,” answered the Tree; “but it is so terrible that I dare not tell it to you.”
“Tell it to me,” said the Nightingale, “I am not afraid.”

“If you want a red rose,” said the Tree, “you must build it out of music by moonlight, and stain it with your own heart’s-blood.  You must sing to me with your breast against a thorn.  All night long you must sing to me, and the thorn must pierce your heart, and your life-blood must flow into my veins, and become mine.”

“Death is a great price to pay for a red rose,” cried the Nightingale, “and Life is very dear to all.  It is pleasant to sit in the green wood, and to watch the Sun in his chariot of gold, and the Moon in her chariot of pearl.  Sweet is the scent of the hawthorn, and sweet are the bluebells that hide in the valley, and the heather that blows on the hill.  Yet Love is better than Life, and what is the heart of a bird compared to the heart of a man?”
So she spread her brown wings for flight, and soared into the air.  She swept over the garden like a shadow, and like a shadow she sailed through the grove.
The young Student was still lying on the grass, where she had left him, and the tears were not yet dry in his beautiful eyes.

“Be happy,” cried the Nightingale, “be happy; you shall have your red rose.  I will build it out of music by moonlight, and stain it with my own heart’s-blood.  All that I ask of you in return is that you will be a true lover, for Love is wiser than Philosophy, though she is wise, and mightier than Power, though he is mighty.  Flame-coloured are his wings, and coloured like flame is his body.  His lips are sweet as honey, and his breath is like frankincense.”
The Student looked up from the grass, and listened, but he could not understand what the Nightingale was saying to him, for he only knew the things that are written down in books.
But the Oak-tree understood, and felt sad, for he was very fond of the little Nightingale who had built her nest in his branches.
“Sing me one last song,” he whispered; “I shall feel very lonely when you are gone.”
So the Nightingale sang to the Oak-tree, and her voice was like water bubbling from a silver jar.
When she had finished her song the Student got up, and pulled a note-book and a lead-pencil out of his pocket.

“She has form,” he said to himself, as he walked away through the grove—“that cannot be denied to her; but has she got feeling?  I am afraid not.  In fact, she is like most artists; she is all style, without any sincerity.  She would not sacrifice herself for others.  She thinks merely of music, and everybody knows that the arts are selfish.  Still, it must be admitted that she has some beautiful notes in her voice.  What a pity it is that they do not mean anything, or do any practical good.” And he went into his room, and lay down on his little pallet-bed, and began to think of his love; and, after a time, he fell asleep.

And when the Moon shone in the heavens the Nightingale flew to the Rose-tree, and set her breast against the thorn.  All night long she sang with her breast against the thorn, and the cold crystal Moon leaned down and listened.  All night long she sang, and the thorn went deeper and deeper into her breast, and her life-blood ebbed away from her.

She sang first of the birth of love in the heart of a boy and a girl. And on the top-most spray of the Rose-tree there blossomed a marvellous rose, petal following petal, as song followed song.  Pale was it, at first, as the mist that hangs over the river—pale as the feet of the morning, and silver as the wings of the dawn.  As the shadow of a rose in a mirror of silver, as the shadow of a rose in a water-pool, so was the rose that blossomed on the topmost spray of the Tree.
But the Tree cried to the Nightingale to press closer against the thorn. “Press closer, little Nightingale,” cried the Tree, “or the Day will come before the rose is finished.”
So the Nightingale pressed closer against the thorn, and louder and louder grew her song, for she sang of the birth of passion in the soul of a man and a maid.

And a delicate flush of pink came into the leaves of the rose, like the flush in the face of the bridegroom when he kisses the lips of the bride. But the thorn had not yet reached her heart, so the rose’s heart remained white, for only a Nightingale’s heart’s-blood can crimson the heart of a rose.
And the Tree cried to the Nightingale to press closer against the thorn. “Press closer, little Nightingale,” cried the Tree, “or the Day will come before the rose is finished.”

So the Nightingale pressed closer against the thorn, and the thorn touched her heart, and a fierce pang of pain shot through her.  Bitter, bitter was the pain, and wilder and wilder grew her song, for she sang of the Love that is perfected by Death, of the Love that dies not in the tomb.
And the marvellous rose became crimson, like the rose of the eastern sky. Crimson was the girdle of petals, and crimson as a ruby was the heart.
But the Nightingale’s voice grew fainter, and her little wings began to beat, and a film came over her eyes.  Fainter and fainter grew her song, and she felt something choking her in her throat.

Then she gave one last burst of music.  The white Moon heard it, and she forgot the dawn, and lingered on in the sky.  The red rose heard it, and it trembled all over with ecstasy, and opened its petals to the cold morning air.  Echo bore it to her purple cavern in the hills, and woke the sleeping shepherds from their dreams.  It floated through the reeds of the river, and they carried its message to the sea.
“Look, look!” cried the Tree, “the rose is finished now”; but the Nightingale made no answer, for she was lying dead in the long grass, with the thorn in her heart.
And at noon the Student opened his window and looked out.

“Why, what a wonderful piece of luck!” he cried; “here is a red rose!  I have never seen any rose like it in all my life.  It is so beautiful that I am sure it has a long Latin name”; and he leaned down and plucked it.
Then he put on his hat, and ran up to the Professor’s house with the rose in his hand.
The daughter of the Professor was sitting in the doorway winding blue silk on a reel, and her little dog was lying at her feet.

“You said that you would dance with me if I brought you a red rose,” cried the Student.  “Here is the reddest rose in all the world.  You will wear it to-night next your heart, and as we dance together it will tell you how I love you.”
But the girl frowned.
“I am afraid it will not go with my dress,” she answered; “and, besides, the Chamberlain’s nephew has sent me some real jewels, and everybody knows that jewels cost far more than flowers.”
“Well, upon my word, you are very ungrateful,” said the Student angrily; and he threw the rose into the street, where it fell into the gutter, and a cart-wheel went over it.

“Ungrateful!” said the girl.  “I tell you what, you are very rude; and, after all, who are you?  Only a Student.  Why, I don’t believe you have even got silver buckles to your shoes as the Chamberlain’s nephew has”; and she got up from her chair and went into the house.

“What a silly thing Love is,” said the Student as he walked away.  “It is not half as useful as Logic, for it does not prove anything, and it is always telling one of things that are not going to happen, and making one believe things that are not true.  In fact, it is quite unpractical, and, as in this age to be practical is everything, I shall go back to Philosophy and study Metaphysics.”
So he returned to his room and pulled out a great dusty book, and began to read.
translated_paragraphs: “她说，只要我给她带去红玫瑰，她就肯跟我跳舞，”年轻的学生喊道，“可是我整个花园里，连一朵红玫瑰也没有。”
夜莺在常青橡树的巢里听见了，从叶子间探出头，心里很奇怪。
“满园竟没有一朵红玫瑰！”他喊着，美丽的眼睛里蓄满了泪水。“唉，人的幸福竟系在这样小小的东西上！贤人们写的书我都读过了，哲学中的奥秘我也全知道了，就为缺一朵红玫瑰，我的日子竟这么苦。”
“我总算见到一个真正的有情人了。”夜莺说，“一夜又一夜，我都歌唱他，虽然我并不认识他。一夜又一夜，我都把他的故事讲给星星听，如今我看见他了。他的头发像风信子花那样浓黑，嘴唇像他渴求的玫瑰那样鲜红。可是热恋把他的脸庞变成了苍白的象牙，忧愁已在他眉间留下印记。”
“明晚，王子要开舞会，”年轻的学生低声说，“我心爱的人也会去。只要带给她一朵红玫瑰，她就会和我一起跳到天亮。只要带给她一朵红玫瑰，我就能搂住她，她会把头靠在我肩上，我会把她的手握在手里。可是我的花园没有红玫瑰，我只好孤零零坐着，看她从身边经过。她理也不会理我，我的心都要碎了。”
“这真是个有情人，”夜莺说，“我歌唱的事，他正亲身受着。于我是快乐，于他却是痛苦。爱情果然是件奇妙的东西！它比祖母绿珍贵，比上好的蛋白石还值钱。用珍珠和石榴都买不到它，集市上也找不着它。商贩卖不了它，天平也称不出多少金子能换它。”
“乐师们会坐在楼廊上，”年轻的学生说，“奏着弦乐。我心爱的人会随着竖琴和小提琴起舞。她会跳得那样轻，脚尖连地板也碰不到。穿着鲜艳礼服的朝臣们会把她团团围住。可是她不会跟我跳，因为我没有红玫瑰给她。”他一下子伏倒在草地上，把脸埋进手里，哭了起来。
“他哭什么呀？”一只小绿蜥蜴翘着尾巴从他身边跑过，开口问道。
“可不是，为什么呢？”一只追逐阳光的蝴蝶扑闪着翅膀说。
“是呀，为什么呢？”一朵雏菊轻声细气地问身旁的花。
“他为一朵红玫瑰哭呢。”夜莺说。
“为一朵红玫瑰？”它们叫起来，“这也太可笑啦！”小蜥蜴向来爱讥讽，索性大声笑了出来。
夜莺却懂得学生悲伤的秘密。她默默坐在橡树上，想着爱情这深奥的事。
忽然，她张开褐色的双翅，高高飞起。她像一道影子穿过小树林，又像一道影子滑过花园。
草坪正中长着一株漂亮的玫瑰。夜莺瞧见了，便飞过去，落在一根细枝上。
“给我一朵红玫瑰吧，”她喊道，“我愿把我最动听的歌儿唱给你。”
玫瑰树却摇摇头。
“我的花是白的，”它说，“白得像海上的浪沫，比山上的雪更白。去找绕着那座旧日晷生长的兄弟吧，说不定它能给你想要的东西。”
夜莺便飞去找绕着旧日晷生长的那株玫瑰。
“给我一朵红玫瑰吧，”她喊道，“我愿把我最动听的歌儿唱给你。”
玫瑰树却摇摇头。
“我的花是黄的，”它说，“黄得像坐在琥珀宝座上的人鱼姑娘的头发。割草人还没提着长镰过来时，草地上那黄水仙也不如它黄。去找长在学生窗下的兄弟吧，说不定它能给你想要的东西。”
夜莺便飞去找长在学生窗下的那株玫瑰。
“给我一朵红玫瑰吧，”她喊道，“我愿把我最动听的歌儿唱给你。”
玫瑰树却摇摇头。
“我的花是红的，”它说，“红得像鸽子的双脚，比海底洞穴里摇了又摇的大扇珊瑚还红。可是寒冬冻冷了我的血管，霜打坏了我的花苞，风暴折断了我的枝条。今年我一朵玫瑰也开不出来。”
“我要的只是一朵红玫瑰呀，”夜莺喊道，“只要一朵！难道没有办法让我得到它吗？”
“倒有一个办法，”玫瑰树说，“可太可怕了，我不敢告诉你。”
“告诉我吧，”夜莺说，“我不怕。”
“你若想要红玫瑰，”树说，“就得在月光下用歌声把它造出来，再用自己的心血把它染红。你得让胸脯抵着一根刺，唱给我听。你得唱整整一夜，让刺扎进你的心，让维系你生命的血流进我的血管，变成我的血。”
“为一朵红玫瑰献出性命，这个价钱真高呀，”夜莺喊道，“活着，谁不觉得可贵呢！坐在绿林里，看太阳乘着金车、月亮乘着珍珠车，多么快活。山楂花的香气多甜，藏在山谷里的蓝铃花，还有山坡上开着的石南，也一样芬芳。可是爱情胜过生命，同一个人的心相比，一只鸟儿的心又算得了什么？”
她张开褐色的双翅，高高飞起。她像一道影子掠过花园，又像一道影子滑进小树林。
年轻的学生仍躺在原先那块草地上，美丽眼睛里的泪还没有干。
“快活起来吧，”夜莺喊道，“快活起来，你会有红玫瑰的。我要在月光下用歌声造出它，用自己的心血把它染红。我只求你给我一样回报。愿你做个真正的有情人。哲学诚然聪慧，爱情比她更聪慧。权势诚然强大，爱情比他更强大。爱情的翅膀是火焰的颜色，身躯也是火焰的颜色。他的嘴唇甜如蜂蜜，气息香如乳香。”
学生在草地上仰起脸来听着，却听不懂夜莺对他说的话，因为他只懂得那些已经写进书里的事。
橡树却懂得了，心里很悲伤。他多么疼爱这只把巢筑在自己枝条间的小夜莺。
“最后再给我唱一支歌吧，”他小声说，“你走了，我会很寂寞。”
夜莺便为橡树唱起歌来，她的歌喉像清泉从一只银罐里汩汩流出。
她唱完之后，学生站起身，从衣袋里摸出一本笔记簿和一支铅笔。
“她倒是懂得形式，”他穿过小树林，边走边对自己说，“这一点不能否认，可她有感情吗？恐怕没有。其实她跟大多数艺术家一样，通身只有风格，毫无真诚可言。她才不会为别人牺牲自己。她满脑子只有音乐，谁都知道，艺术总是自私的。不过得承认，她的嗓子有几个音唱得是好听。可惜没什么意思，也派不上实际用场。”他回到房间，躺在那张简陋的小床上，想着心爱的姑娘，过了一会儿就睡着了。
月亮照亮天空时，夜莺飞向玫瑰树，把胸脯贴上了刺。整整一夜，她抵着刺歌唱，冷水晶似的月亮俯身倾听。整整一夜，她不停地唱，刺一寸寸扎进她的胸口，她的生命随着鲜血一点点流走。
她先唱爱情怎样在一个男孩和一个女孩心里萌生。玫瑰树最高的枝梢上，开出了一朵奇异的玫瑰。歌儿一支接一支，花瓣也一片接一片地舒展开来。起初，花色淡如河上悬着的雾，淡如清晨的足尖，银亮如黎明的翅膀。像银镜里一朵玫瑰的影子，又像水潭里一朵玫瑰的影子。最高的枝梢上，那朵玫瑰就是这样。
玫瑰树却叫夜莺再往刺上靠一靠。“靠紧些，小夜莺！”它喊着，“不然花还没开好，天就已经亮啦。”
夜莺便又往刺上紧贴了一点，歌声越来越响亮。她唱起热烈的爱怎样在一个青年和一个少女的心灵里萌生。
花瓣上浮起一抹温柔的粉红，像新郎亲吻新娘时脸上泛起的红晕。可那刺还没碰到夜莺的心，花心便仍是白的，因为只有夜莺心头的血，才能把玫瑰的花心染成深红。
玫瑰树又叫夜莺再往刺上靠一靠。“靠紧些，小夜莺！”它喊着，“不然花还没开好，天就已经亮啦。”
夜莺便又往刺上贴紧了些。刺碰到了她的心，一阵剧痛穿过全身。痛啊，好痛，她的歌声却越发激荡。她唱那在死亡中圆满的爱，唱那到了坟墓里也不死的爱。
那朵奇异的玫瑰变成了深红，像东方天际的一抹玫瑰红。围成一圈的花瓣深红，花心也红得像一枚红宝石。
可夜莺的声音渐渐弱了，小翅膀开始扑动，眼睛上蒙了一层薄雾。她的歌声越来越轻，她感觉有什么东西哽住了喉咙。
随即，她迸出最后一串歌声。白月亮听见了，忘了黎明，还留恋在天上。红玫瑰听见了，欢喜得浑身颤抖，朝着清冷的晨风打开了花瓣。回声把歌声捎进山间紫色的洞穴，从梦中唤醒熟睡的牧羊人。歌声又飘过河里的芦苇，芦苇把它的消息传给了海洋。
“快看，快看！”玫瑰树喊道，“玫瑰终于开好啦！”夜莺却没有回答。她躺在长草间，已经死了，那根刺还留在她的心里。
到了中午，学生推开窗户，探头向外看。
“哎呀，哪来这样好的运气！”他叫道，“这里有一朵红玫瑰！我这辈子也没见过这样的玫瑰。长得这么美，准有一个老长的拉丁名字。”他俯下身，摘了花。
他戴上帽子，手拿玫瑰，一路跑到教授家。
教授的女儿坐在门口，正把蓝丝线绕上线轴，她的小狗趴在她脚边。
“你说过我要是给你带来一朵红玫瑰，你就肯和我跳舞，”学生喊道，“瞧，这是全世界最红的玫瑰。今晚你把它戴在心口，和我一起跳舞的时候，它就会告诉你我有多爱你。”
姑娘却皱起了眉。
“恐怕跟我的裙子不配，”她答道，“再说，宫廷总管的侄子给我送来了真宝石。谁都知道，宝石比鲜花贵得多。”
“说实话，你真不懂得感激！”学生气愤地说，一把将玫瑰扔到街上。花滚进排水沟，一只车轮从上面轧了过去。
“不懂得感激？”姑娘说，“我还要告诉你，你真没礼貌！说到底，你是谁呀？不过是个学生。我看你的鞋子连银搭扣都没有。宫廷总管的侄子就有！”她从椅子上站起来，进了屋。
“爱情真是个蠢东西，”学生边走边说，“论用处，还赶不上逻辑学的一半。它什么也证明不了，成天说些不会发生的事，叫人相信不是真的东西。说到底，它一点儿也不实用。眼下这个年头，实用比什么都要紧。我还是回去学哲学，研究形而上学吧。”
于是他回房抽出一本落满灰尘的大部头书，开始读了起来。

source_paragraphs: EVERY afternoon, as they were coming from school, the children used to go and play in the Giant’s garden.

It was a large lovely garden, with soft green grass.  Here and there over the grass stood beautiful flowers like stars, and there were twelve peach-trees that in the spring-time broke out into delicate blossoms of pink and pearl, and in the autumn bore rich fruit.  The birds sat on the trees and sang so sweetly that the children used to stop their games in order to listen to them.  “How happy we are here!” they cried to each other.

One day the Giant came back.  He had been to visit his friend the Cornish ogre, and had stayed with him for seven years.  After the seven years were over he had said all that he had to say, for his conversation was limited, and he determined to return to his own castle.  When he arrived he saw the children playing in the garden.
“What are you doing here?” he cried in a very gruff voice, and the children ran away.
“My own garden is my own garden,” said the Giant; “any one can understand that, and I will allow nobody to play in it but myself.”  So he built a high wall all round it, and put up a notice-board.
TRESPASSERS
WILL BE
PROSECUTED
He was a very selfish Giant.

The poor children had now nowhere to play.  They tried to play on the road, but the road was very dusty and full of hard stones, and they did not like it.  They used to wander round the high wall when their lessons were over, and talk about the beautiful garden inside.  “How happy we were there,” they said to each other.

Then the Spring came, and all over the country there were little blossoms and little birds.  Only in the garden of the Selfish Giant it was still winter.  The birds did not care to sing in it as there were no children, and the trees forgot to blossom.  Once a beautiful flower put its head out from the grass, but when it saw the notice-board it was so sorry for the children that it slipped back into the ground again, and went off to sleep.  The only people who were pleased were the Snow and the Frost. “Spring has forgotten this garden,” they cried, “so we will live here all the year round.”  The Snow covered up the grass with her great white cloak, and the Frost painted all the trees silver.  Then they invited the North Wind to stay with them, and he came.  He was wrapped in furs, and he roared all day about the garden, and blew the chimney-pots down. “This is a delightful spot,” he said, “we must ask the Hail on a visit.” So the Hail came.  Every day for three hours he rattled on the roof of the castle till he broke most of the slates, and then he ran round and round the garden as fast as he could go.  He was dressed in grey, and his breath was like ice.
“I cannot understand why the Spring is so late in coming,” said the Selfish Giant, as he sat at the window and looked out at his cold white garden; “I hope there will be a change in the weather.”

But the Spring never came, nor the Summer.  The Autumn gave golden fruit to every garden, but to the Giant’s garden she gave none.  “He is too selfish,” she said.  So it was always Winter there, and the North Wind, and the Hail, and the Frost, and the Snow danced about through the trees.

One morning the Giant was lying awake in bed when he heard some lovely music.  It sounded so sweet to his ears that he thought it must be the King’s musicians passing by.  It was really only a little linnet singing outside his window, but it was so long since he had heard a bird sing in his garden that it seemed to him to be the most beautiful music in the world.  Then the Hail stopped dancing over his head, and the North Wind ceased roaring, and a delicious perfume came to him through the open casement.  “I believe the Spring has come at last,” said the Giant; and he jumped out of bed and looked out.
What did he see?

He saw a most wonderful sight.  Through a little hole in the wall the children had crept in, and they were sitting in the branches of the trees.  In every tree that he could see there was a little child.  And the trees were so glad to have the children back again that they had covered themselves with blossoms, and were waving their arms gently above the children’s heads.  The birds were flying about and twittering with delight, and the flowers were looking up through the green grass and laughing.  It was a lovely scene, only in one corner it was still winter. It was the farthest corner of the garden, and in it was standing a little boy.  He was so small that he could not reach up to the branches of the tree, and he was wandering all round it, crying bitterly.  The poor tree was still quite covered with frost and snow, and the North Wind was blowing and roaring above it.  “Climb up! little boy,” said the Tree, and it bent its branches down as low as it could; but the boy was too tiny.

And the Giant’s heart melted as he looked out.  “How selfish I have been!” he said; “now I know why the Spring would not come here.  I will put that poor little boy on the top of the tree, and then I will knock down the wall, and my garden shall be the children’s playground for ever and ever.”  He was really very sorry for what he had done.

So he crept downstairs and opened the front door quite softly, and went out into the garden.  But when the children saw him they were so frightened that they all ran away, and the garden became winter again. Only the little boy did not run, for his eyes were so full of tears that he did not see the Giant coming.  And the Giant stole up behind him and took him gently in his hand, and put him up into the tree.  And the tree broke at once into blossom, and the birds came and sang on it, and the little boy stretched out his two arms and flung them round the Giant’s neck, and kissed him.  And the other children, when they saw that the Giant was not wicked any longer, came running back, and with them came the Spring.  “It is your garden now, little children,” said the Giant, and he took a great axe and knocked down the wall.  And when the people were going to market at twelve o’clock they found the Giant playing with the children in the most beautiful garden they had ever seen.
All day long they played, and in the evening they came to the Giant to bid him good-bye.
“But where is your little companion?” he said: “the boy I put into the tree.”  The Giant loved him the best because he had kissed him.
“We don’t know,” answered the children; “he has gone away.”
“You must tell him to be sure and come here to-morrow,” said the Giant. But the children said that they did not know where he lived, and had never seen him before; and the Giant felt very sad.

Every afternoon, when school was over, the children came and played with the Giant.  But the little boy whom the Giant loved was never seen again. The Giant was very kind to all the children, yet he longed for his first little friend, and often spoke of him.  “How I would like to see him!” he used to say.

Years went over, and the Giant grew very old and feeble.  He could not play about any more, so he sat in a huge armchair, and watched the children at their games, and admired his garden.  “I have many beautiful flowers,” he said; “but the children are the most beautiful flowers of all.”
One winter morning he looked out of his window as he was dressing.  He did not hate the Winter now, for he knew that it was merely the Spring asleep, and that the flowers were resting.

Suddenly he rubbed his eyes in wonder, and looked and looked.  It certainly was a marvellous sight.  In the farthest corner of the garden was a tree quite covered with lovely white blossoms.  Its branches were all golden, and silver fruit hung down from them, and underneath it stood the little boy he had loved.

Downstairs ran the Giant in great joy, and out into the garden.  He hastened across the grass, and came near to the child.  And when he came quite close his face grew red with anger, and he said, “Who hath dared to wound thee?”  For on the palms of the child’s hands were the prints of two nails, and the prints of two nails were on the little feet.
“Who hath dared to wound thee?” cried the Giant; “tell me, that I may take my big sword and slay him.”
“Nay!” answered the child; “but these are the wounds of Love.”
“Who art thou?” said the Giant, and a strange awe fell on him, and he knelt before the little child.
And the child smiled on the Giant, and said to him, “You let me play once in your garden, to-day you shall come with me to my garden, which is Paradise.”
And when the children ran in that afternoon, they found the Giant lying dead under the tree, all covered with white blossoms.
translated_paragraphs: 每天下午放了学，孩子们总要去巨人的花园里玩。
那是一座又大又美的花园，青草柔软，绿油油的。草丛里这里一朵、那里一朵，漂亮的花儿像星星。还有十二棵桃树，春天一到，细嫩的花开满枝头，粉红和珠白的颜色映在一起。秋天，枝头便结满丰美的果实。鸟儿停在树上，歌声太好听，孩子们常常停下游戏来听。“在这里多快活呀！”他们彼此喊道。
有一天，巨人回来了。他先前去看一位朋友，那是个住在康沃尔的食人怪。巨人在他家一住就是七年。七年过去，他要说的话都说完了，本来他的话也不多。于是他决定回自己的城堡。一到家，就看见孩子们正在花园里玩。

“你们在这儿做什么？”他粗声粗气地大喊。孩子们逃走了。“我的花园就是我的花园。这一点谁都懂。除了我自己，我不许任何人在里头玩。”他在花园四周砌了一圈高墙，挂起一块牌子，上面写着：

擅闯者
一律
追诉
他是一个非常自私的巨人。
可怜的孩子们没有地方玩了。他们试着在路上玩，可路面灰扑扑的，到处都是硬石头，一点也不好玩。放了学，他们常绕着高墙慢慢走，谈起墙里那个美丽的花园。“从前在里头玩，多快活呀。”他们对彼此说。
后来春天来了，满乡的小花开了，小鸟也来了。唯独自私巨人的花园里还是冬天。那里没有孩子，鸟儿没兴趣进去唱歌，树也忘记了开花。有一次，一朵漂亮的花刚从草里探出头，就看见了那块牌子。她心疼那些孩子，于是又缩回地下睡觉去了。

高兴的只有雪和霜。“春天把这园子忘啦，”她们喊道，“咱们一整年都可以住在这里。”雪张开宽大的白斗篷，盖住草地。霜把每一棵树都涂成了银色。她们邀北风来住，他果然来了，裹着皮毛，整天在园中吼叫，把烟囱顶都吹了下来。“这地方真叫人欢喜，”北风说，“得把冰雹也请来玩。”冰雹便来了。每天他都在城堡屋顶上噼里啪啦地敲，敲足三个钟头，敲坏了大半的石瓦，再到花园里用最快的速度绕圈子跑。他一身灰衣裳，嘴里呼出的气像冰一样冷。
“真想不通，春天今年怎么来得这么迟。”自私的巨人坐在窗边，望着冰冷雪白的花园说，“但愿天气快有些变化。”
可是春天一直没来，夏天也没来。秋天送给每一座花园金黄色的果实，唯独没给巨人的花园一个。“他太自私了。”她说。所以这里一直是冬天，北风、冰雹、霜和雪在树丛中跳着舞。
一天早晨，巨人醒了，正躺在床上，忽然听见一阵好听的音乐。那声音太美了，他以为是国王的乐队从门外经过。其实只有一只小红雀，在他的窗外唱着歌儿。可是已经好久好久，他没在自己的园子里听过鸟叫了，因此他觉得这是世间最美的乐声。头顶上，冰雹不再跳舞，北风也不再咆哮。一阵芬芳从敞开的窗子飘了进来。“我想，春天总算来啦！”巨人跳下床，朝外望去。
他看见了什么呢？
那真是一个奇妙极了的景象。孩子们从墙上的小洞钻进了花园，正坐在枝桠上。放眼望去，每一棵树上都坐着一个小孩子。树木欢喜极了，孩子们可算回来了！它们全身都开满了花，还在孩子们头顶轻轻挥动枝条做的手臂。鸟儿快活地叫着，飞来飞去，花儿从绿草里仰起头来笑。
满园都这样好看，只有一个角落还留在冬天里。那是离他最远的角落，有个小男孩站在那儿。他太矮了，伸手够不着树枝，只好绕着树转，伤心地哭个不停。那棵可怜的树从头到脚裹着霜雪，北风在上面呼呼地吹。“爬上来吧，小男孩。”树说。它已经尽力把枝条垂到最低了，可那孩子实在太小。
巨人望着这一切，心软了下来。“我先前多自私啊！”他说，“现在我明白春天为什么不肯进来了。我要把那可怜的小男孩抱到树梢上，还要拆掉那堵墙。从今以后，我的花园永永远远是孩子们玩耍的地方。”他真的十分懊悔自己做过的事。
他踮着脚走下楼，轻轻推开大门，进了花园。孩子们一看见他，还是吓得全跑掉了，园子里立刻又变成冬天。只有那个小男孩没逃跑。泪水装满了他的眼睛，他没看见巨人走来。巨人悄悄绕到他身后，用手轻轻托住他，把他放上树。花一下子开满了树，鸟儿飞来，在枝头唱歌。小男孩伸出两只胳膊，紧紧搂住巨人的脖子，亲了他一下。别的孩子一看巨人不再那么凶恶，便又跑回来了。跟他们一起回来的，还有春天。
“小朋友们，现在这是你们的花园啦！”巨人说。他抡起一把大斧头，把墙拆掉了。中午十二点，赶集的人经过，看见巨人和孩子们玩在一起，那是他们见过的最美的花园。
他们玩了一整天，傍晚，孩子们跑来跟巨人道别。
“可你们那位小伙伴呢？”他说，“就是我抱上树的那个小男孩。”巨人最惦记他，因为他吻过自己。“我们不知道，”孩子们说，“他走了。”“一定要告诉他，明天还要来。”巨人说。可孩子们说，他们不知道他住在哪儿，从前也从没见过他。巨人很是难过。
每天下午放学，孩子们都来和巨人玩。巨人心爱的那个小男孩，却一直没有再出现。他对所有的孩子都很好，心里还是思念那位最早跟他交上朋友的小家伙，总提起他：“多想再见他一面啊！”
一年又一年，巨人渐渐老了，身子衰弱，再不能跟着孩子跑来跑去。他就坐在大扶手椅上，看孩子们做游戏，欣赏自己的花园。“我有许多漂亮的花，”他说，“不过，最美的花是孩子们。”
一个冬天的早晨，他边穿衣服边向窗外瞧。他如今不讨厌冬天了，他知道，那只是春天睡着了，花儿正在歇息。
忽然，他诧异地揉了揉眼睛，看了又看。真是奇景！花园最远的角落，一棵树开满了可爱的白花。枝条全是金的，枝上垂着银色的果子，树底下就站着他心爱的那个小男孩。
巨人欢喜地奔下楼，跑进花园。他急急穿过草地，走近那孩子。可等到了近前，他气得满脸通红：“是谁胆敢伤害你？”孩子的两手掌心各有一个钉痕，两只小脚上也各有一个。
“是谁胆敢伤害你？”巨人叫道，“告诉我，我要拔出大剑去杀了那个人！”
“不，”孩子答道，“这是爱的伤痕。”
“你是谁？”巨人问。一种奇异的敬畏涌上心头，他在小孩子面前跪了下来。
孩子朝他微笑，说：“有一次，你让我在你的花园里玩。今天，你也跟我到我的花园去吧。我的花园就是天堂。”
那天下午，孩子们跑进园子时，发现巨人已静静地死在树下，身上落满了白花。

source_paragraphs: ONE morning the old Water-rat put his head out of his hole.  He had bright beady eyes and stiff grey whiskers and his tail was like a long bit of black india-rubber.  The little ducks were swimming about in the pond, looking just like a lot of yellow canaries, and their mother, who was pure white with real red legs, was trying to teach them how to stand on their heads in the water.

“You will never be in the best society unless you can stand on your heads,” she kept saying to them; and every now and then she showed them how it was done.  But the little ducks paid no attention to her.  They were so young that they did not know what an advantage it is to be in society at all.
“What disobedient children!” cried the old Water-rat; “they really deserve to be drowned.”
“Nothing of the kind,” answered the Duck, “every one must make a beginning, and parents cannot be too patient.”

“Ah! I know nothing about the feelings of parents,” said the Water-rat; “I am not a family man.  In fact, I have never been married, and I never intend to be.  Love is all very well in its way, but friendship is much higher.  Indeed, I know of nothing in the world that is either nobler or rarer than a devoted friendship.”
“And what, pray, is your idea of the duties of a devoted friend?” asked a Green Linnet, who was sitting in a willow-tree hard by, and had overheard the conversation.
“Yes, that is just what I want to know,” said the Duck; and she swam away to the end of the pond, and stood upon her head, in order to give her children a good example.
“What a silly question!” cried the Water-rat.  “I should expect my devoted friend to be devoted to me, of course.”
“And what would you do in return?” said the little bird, swinging upon a silver spray, and flapping his tiny wings.
“I don’t understand you,” answered the Water-rat.
“Let me tell you a story on the subject,” said the Linnet.
“Is the story about me?” asked the Water-rat.  “If so, I will listen to it, for I am extremely fond of fiction.”
“It is applicable to you,” answered the Linnet; and he flew down, and alighting upon the bank, he told the story of The Devoted Friend.
“Once upon a time,” said the Linnet, “there was an honest little fellow named Hans.”
“Was he very distinguished?” asked the Water-rat.

“No,” answered the Linnet, “I don’t think he was distinguished at all, except for his kind heart, and his funny round good-humoured face.  He lived in a tiny cottage all by himself, and every day he worked in his garden.  In all the country-side there was no garden so lovely as his. Sweet-william grew there, and Gilly-flowers, and Shepherds’-purses, and Fair-maids of France.  There were damask Roses, and yellow Roses, lilac Crocuses, and gold, purple Violets and white.  Columbine and Ladysmock, Marjoram and Wild Basil, the Cowslip and the Flower-de-luce, the Daffodil and the Clove-Pink bloomed or blossomed in their proper order as the months went by, one flower taking another flower’s place, so that there were always beautiful things to look at, and pleasant odours to smell.

“Little Hans had a great many friends, but the most devoted friend of all was big Hugh the Miller.  Indeed, so devoted was the rich Miller to little Hans, that he would never go by his garden without leaning over the wall and plucking a large nosegay, or a handful of sweet herbs, or filling his pockets with plums and cherries if it was the fruit season.
“‘Real friends should have everything in common,’ the Miller used to say, and little Hans nodded and smiled, and felt very proud of having a friend with such noble ideas.

“Sometimes, indeed, the neighbours thought it strange that the rich Miller never gave little Hans anything in return, though he had a hundred sacks of flour stored away in his mill, and six milch cows, and a large flock of woolly sheep; but Hans never troubled his head about these things, and nothing gave him greater pleasure than to listen to all the wonderful things the Miller used to say about the unselfishness of true friendship.

“So little Hans worked away in his garden.  During the spring, the summer, and the autumn he was very happy, but when the winter came, and he had no fruit or flowers to bring to the market, he suffered a good deal from cold and hunger, and often had to go to bed without any supper but a few dried pears or some hard nuts.  In the winter, also, he was extremely lonely, as the Miller never came to see him then.

“‘There is no good in my going to see little Hans as long as the snow lasts,’ the Miller used to say to his wife, ‘for when people are in trouble they should be left alone, and not be bothered by visitors.  That at least is my idea about friendship, and I am sure I am right.  So I shall wait till the spring comes, and then I shall pay him a visit, and he will be able to give me a large basket of primroses and that will make him so happy.’

“‘You are certainly very thoughtful about others,’ answered the Wife, as she sat in her comfortable armchair by the big pinewood fire; ‘very thoughtful indeed.  It is quite a treat to hear you talk about friendship.  I am sure the clergyman himself could not say such beautiful things as you do, though he does live in a three-storied house, and wear a gold ring on his little finger.’
“‘But could we not ask little Hans up here?’ said the Miller’s youngest son.  ‘If poor Hans is in trouble I will give him half my porridge, and show him my white rabbits.’

“‘What a silly boy you are!’ cried the Miller; ‘I really don’t know what is the use of sending you to school.  You seem not to learn anything. Why, if little Hans came up here, and saw our warm fire, and our good supper, and our great cask of red wine, he might get envious, and envy is a most terrible thing, and would spoil anybody’s nature.  I certainly will not allow Hans’ nature to be spoiled.  I am his best friend, and I will always watch over him, and see that he is not led into any temptations.  Besides, if Hans came here, he might ask me to let him have some flour on credit, and that I could not do.  Flour is one thing, and friendship is another, and they should not be confused.  Why, the words are spelt differently, and mean quite different things.  Everybody can see that.’
“‘How well you talk!’ said the Miller’s Wife, pouring herself out a large glass of warm ale; ‘really I feel quite drowsy.  It is just like being in church.’

“‘Lots of people act well,’ answered the Miller; ‘but very few people talk well, which shows that talking is much the more difficult thing of the two, and much the finer thing also’; and he looked sternly across the table at his little son, who felt so ashamed of himself that he hung his head down, and grew quite scarlet, and began to cry into his tea. However, he was so young that you must excuse him.”
“Is that the end of the story?” asked the Water-rat.
“Certainly not,” answered the Linnet, “that is the beginning.”

“Then you are quite behind the age,” said the Water-rat.  “Every good story-teller nowadays starts with the end, and then goes on to the beginning, and concludes with the middle.  That is the new method.  I heard all about it the other day from a critic who was walking round the pond with a young man.  He spoke of the matter at great length, and I am sure he must have been right, for he had blue spectacles and a bald head, and whenever the young man made any remark, he always answered ‘Pooh!’ But pray go on with your story.  I like the Miller immensely.  I have all kinds of beautiful sentiments myself, so there is a great sympathy between us.”

“Well,” said the Linnet, hopping now on one leg and now on the other, “as soon as the winter was over, and the primroses began to open their pale yellow stars, the Miller said to his wife that he would go down and see little Hans.
“‘Why, what a good heart you have!’ cried his Wife; ‘you are always thinking of others.  And mind you take the big basket with you for the flowers.’
“So the Miller tied the sails of the windmill together with a strong iron chain, and went down the hill with the basket on his arm.
“‘Good morning, little Hans,’ said the Miller.
“‘Good morning,’ said Hans, leaning on his spade, and smiling from ear to ear.
“‘And how have you been all the winter?’ said the Miller.

“‘Well, really,’ cried Hans, ‘it is very good of you to ask, very good indeed.  I am afraid I had rather a hard time of it, but now the spring has come, and I am quite happy, and all my flowers are doing well.’
“‘We often talked of you during the winter, Hans,’ said the Miller, ‘and wondered how you were getting on.’
“‘That was kind of you,’ said Hans; ‘I was half afraid you had forgotten me.’

“‘Hans, I am surprised at you,’ said the Miller; ‘friendship never forgets.  That is the wonderful thing about it, but I am afraid you don’t understand the poetry of life.  How lovely your primroses are looking, by-the-bye!”

“‘They are certainly very lovely,’ said Hans, ‘and it is a most lucky thing for me that I have so many.  I am going to bring them into the market and sell them to the Burgomaster’s daughter, and buy back my wheelbarrow with the money.’
“‘Buy back your wheelbarrow?  You don’t mean to say you have sold it? What a very stupid thing to do!’

“‘Well, the fact is,’ said Hans, ‘that I was obliged to.  You see the winter was a very bad time for me, and I really had no money at all to buy bread with.  So I first sold the silver buttons off my Sunday coat, and then I sold my silver chain, and then I sold my big pipe, and at last I sold my wheelbarrow.  But I am going to buy them all back again now.’

“‘Hans,’ said the Miller, ‘I will give you my wheelbarrow.  It is not in very good repair; indeed, one side is gone, and there is something wrong with the wheel-spokes; but in spite of that I will give it to you.  I know it is very generous of me, and a great many people would think me extremely foolish for parting with it, but I am not like the rest of the world.  I think that generosity is the essence of friendship, and, besides, I have got a new wheelbarrow for myself.  Yes, you may set your mind at ease, I will give you my wheelbarrow.’
“‘Well, really, that is generous of you,’ said little Hans, and his funny round face glowed all over with pleasure.  ‘I can easily put it in repair, as I have a plank of wood in the house.’

“‘A plank of wood!’ said the Miller; ‘why, that is just what I want for the roof of my barn.  There is a very large hole in it, and the corn will all get damp if I don’t stop it up.  How lucky you mentioned it!  It is quite remarkable how one good action always breeds another.  I have given you my wheelbarrow, and now you are going to give me your plank.  Of course, the wheelbarrow is worth far more than the plank, but true, friendship never notices things like that.  Pray get it at once, and I will set to work at my barn this very day.’
“‘Certainly,’ cried little Hans, and he ran into the shed and dragged the plank out.

“‘It is not a very big plank,’ said the Miller, looking at it, ‘and I am afraid that after I have mended my barn-roof there won’t be any left for you to mend the wheelbarrow with; but, of course, that is not my fault. And now, as I have given you my wheelbarrow, I am sure you would like to give me some flowers in return.  Here is the basket, and mind you fill it quite full.’

“‘Quite full?’ said little Hans, rather sorrowfully, for it was really a very big basket, and he knew that if he filled it he would have no flowers left for the market and he was very anxious to get his silver buttons back.

“‘Well, really,’ answered the Miller, ‘as I have given you my wheelbarrow, I don’t think that it is much to ask you for a few flowers. I may be wrong, but I should have thought that friendship, true friendship, was quite free from selfishness of any kind.’

“‘My dear friend, my best friend,’ cried little Hans, ‘you are welcome to all the flowers in my garden.  I would much sooner have your good opinion than my silver buttons, any day’; and he ran and plucked all his pretty primroses, and filled the Miller’s basket.
“‘Good-bye, little Hans,’ said the Miller, as he went up the hill with the plank on his shoulder, and the big basket in his hand.
“‘Good-bye,’ said little Hans, and he began to dig away quite merrily, he was so pleased about the wheelbarrow.

“The next day he was nailing up some honeysuckle against the porch, when he heard the Miller’s voice calling to him from the road.  So he jumped off the ladder, and ran down the garden, and looked over the wall.
“There was the Miller with a large sack of flour on his back.
“‘Dear little Hans,’ said the Miller, ‘would you mind carrying this sack of flour for me to market?’
“‘Oh, I am so sorry,’ said Hans, ‘but I am really very busy to-day.  I have got all my creepers to nail up, and all my flowers to water, and all my grass to roll.’
“‘Well, really,’ said the Miller, ‘I think that, considering that I am going to give you my wheelbarrow, it is rather unfriendly of you to refuse.’
“‘Oh, don’t say that,’ cried little Hans, ‘I wouldn’t be unfriendly for the whole world’; and he ran in for his cap, and trudged off with the big sack on his shoulders.

“It was a very hot day, and the road was terribly dusty, and before Hans had reached the sixth milestone he was so tired that he had to sit down and rest.  However, he went on bravely, and as last he reached the market.  After he had waited there some time, he sold the sack of flour for a very good price, and then he returned home at once, for he was afraid that if he stopped too late he might meet some robbers on the way.

“‘It has certainly been a hard day,’ said little Hans to himself as he was going to bed, ‘but I am glad I did not refuse the Miller, for he is my best friend, and, besides, he is going to give me his wheelbarrow.’
“Early the next morning the Miller came down to get the money for his sack of flour, but little Hans was so tired that he was still in bed.

“‘Upon my word,’ said the Miller, ‘you are very lazy.  Really, considering that I am going to give you my wheelbarrow, I think you might work harder.  Idleness is a great sin, and I certainly don’t like any of my friends to be idle or sluggish.  You must not mind my speaking quite plainly to you.  Of course I should not dream of doing so if I were not your friend.  But what is the good of friendship if one cannot say exactly what one means?  Anybody can say charming things and try to please and to flatter, but a true friend always says unpleasant things, and does not mind giving pain.  Indeed, if he is a really true friend he prefers it, for he knows that then he is doing good.’

“‘I am very sorry,’ said little Hans, rubbing his eyes and pulling off his night-cap, ‘but I was so tired that I thought I would lie in bed for a little time, and listen to the birds singing.  Do you know that I always work better after hearing the birds sing?’
“‘Well, I am glad of that,’ said the Miller, clapping little Hans on the back, ‘for I want you to come up to the mill as soon as you are dressed, and mend my barn-roof for me.’
“Poor little Hans was very anxious to go and work in his garden, for his flowers had not been watered for two days, but he did not like to refuse the Miller, as he was such a good friend to him.
“‘Do you think it would be unfriendly of me if I said I was busy?’ he inquired in a shy and timid voice.
“‘Well, really,’ answered the Miller, ‘I do not think it is much to ask of you, considering that I am going to give you my wheelbarrow; but of course if you refuse I will go and do it myself.’
“‘Oh! on no account,’ cried little Hans and he jumped out of bed, and dressed himself, and went up to the barn.
“He worked there all day long, till sunset, and at sunset the Miller came to see how he was getting on.
“‘Have you mended the hole in the roof yet, little Hans?’ cried the Miller in a cheery voice.
“‘It is quite mended,’ answered little Hans, coming down the ladder.
“‘Ah!’ said the Miller, ‘there is no work so delightful as the work one does for others.’

“‘It is certainly a great privilege to hear you talk,’ answered little Hans, sitting down, and wiping his forehead, ‘a very great privilege. But I am afraid I shall never have such beautiful ideas as you have.’
“‘Oh! they will come to you,’ said the Miller, ‘but you must take more pains.  At present you have only the practice of friendship; some day you will have the theory also.’
“‘Do you really think I shall?’ asked little Hans.
“‘I have no doubt of it,’ answered the Miller, ‘but now that you have mended the roof, you had better go home and rest, for I want you to drive my sheep to the mountain to-morrow.’

“Poor little Hans was afraid to say anything to this, and early the next morning the Miller brought his sheep round to the cottage, and Hans started off with them to the mountain.  It took him the whole day to get there and back; and when he returned he was so tired that he went off to sleep in his chair, and did not wake up till it was broad daylight.
“‘What a delightful time I shall have in my garden,’ he said, and he went to work at once.

“But somehow he was never able to look after his flowers at all, for his friend the Miller was always coming round and sending him off on long errands, or getting him to help at the mill.  Little Hans was very much distressed at times, as he was afraid his flowers would think he had forgotten them, but he consoled himself by the reflection that the Miller was his best friend.  ‘Besides,’ he used to say, ‘he is going to give me his wheelbarrow, and that is an act of pure generosity.’

“So little Hans worked away for the Miller, and the Miller said all kinds of beautiful things about friendship, which Hans took down in a note-book, and used to read over at night, for he was a very good scholar.

“Now it happened that one evening little Hans was sitting by his fireside when a loud rap came at the door.  It was a very wild night, and the wind was blowing and roaring round the house so terribly that at first he thought it was merely the storm.  But a second rap came, and then a third, louder than any of the others.
“‘It is some poor traveller,’ said little Hans to himself, and he ran to the door.
“There stood the Miller with a lantern in one hand and a big stick in the other.

“‘Dear little Hans,’ cried the Miller, ‘I am in great trouble.  My little boy has fallen off a ladder and hurt himself, and I am going for the Doctor.  But he lives so far away, and it is such a bad night, that it has just occurred to me that it would be much better if you went instead of me.  You know I am going to give you my wheelbarrow, and so, it is only fair that you should do something for me in return.’

“‘Certainly,’ cried little Hans, ‘I take it quite as a compliment your coming to me, and I will start off at once.  But you must lend me your lantern, as the night is so dark that I am afraid I might fall into the ditch.’
“‘I am very sorry,’ answered the Miller, ‘but it is my new lantern, and it would be a great loss to me if anything happened to it.’
“‘Well, never mind, I will do without it,’ cried little Hans, and he took down his great fur coat, and his warm scarlet cap, and tied a muffler round his throat, and started off.

“What a dreadful storm it was!  The night was so black that little Hans could hardly see, and the wind was so strong that he could scarcely stand.  However, he was very courageous, and after he had been walking about three hours, he arrived at the Doctor’s house, and knocked at the door.
“‘Who is there?’ cried the Doctor, putting his head out of his bedroom window.
“‘Little Hans, Doctor.’
“’What do you want, little Hans?’
“‘The Miller’s son has fallen from a ladder, and has hurt himself, and the Miller wants you to come at once.’
“‘All right!’ said the Doctor; and he ordered his horse, and his big boots, and his lantern, and came downstairs, and rode off in the direction of the Miller’s house, little Hans trudging behind him.

“But the storm grew worse and worse, and the rain fell in torrents, and little Hans could not see where he was going, or keep up with the horse. At last he lost his way, and wandered off on the moor, which was a very dangerous place, as it was full of deep holes, and there poor little Hans was drowned.  His body was found the next day by some goatherds, floating in a great pool of water, and was brought back by them to the cottage.
“Everybody went to little Hans’ funeral, as he was so popular, and the Miller was the chief mourner.

“‘As I was his best friend,’ said the Miller, ‘it is only fair that I should have the best place’; so he walked at the head of the procession in a long black cloak, and every now and then he wiped his eyes with a big pocket-handkerchief.
“‘Little Hans is certainly a great loss to every one,’ said the Blacksmith, when the funeral was over, and they were all seated comfortably in the inn, drinking spiced wine and eating sweet cakes.

“‘A great loss to me at any rate,’ answered the Miller; ‘why, I had as good as given him my wheelbarrow, and now I really don’t know what to do with it.  It is very much in my way at home, and it is in such bad repair that I could not get anything for it if I sold it.  I will certainly take care not to give away anything again.  One always suffers for being generous.’”
“Well?” said the Water-rat, after a long pause.
“Well, that is the end,” said the Linnet.
“But what became of the Miller?” asked the Water-rat.
“Oh!  I really don’t know,” replied the Linnet; “and I am sure that I don’t care.”
“It is quite evident then that you have no sympathy in your nature,” said the Water-rat.
“I am afraid you don’t quite see the moral of the story,” remarked the Linnet.
“The what?” screamed the Water-rat.
“The moral.”
“Do you mean to say that the story has a moral?”
“Certainly,” said the Linnet.

“Well, really,” said the Water-rat, in a very angry manner, “I think you should have told me that before you began.  If you had done so, I certainly would not have listened to you; in fact, I should have said ‘Pooh,’ like the critic.  However, I can say it now”; so he shouted out “Pooh” at the top of his voice, gave a whisk with his tail, and went back into his hole.

“And how do you like the Water-rat?” asked the Duck, who came paddling up some minutes afterwards.  “He has a great many good points, but for my own part I have a mother’s feelings, and I can never look at a confirmed bachelor without the tears coming into my eyes.”
“I am rather afraid that I have annoyed him,” answered the Linnet.  “The fact is, that I told him a story with a moral.”
“Ah! that is always a very dangerous thing to do,” said the Duck.
And I quite agree with her.
translated_paragraphs: 一天早晨，老水鼠从洞口探出头来。他一双小眼珠亮晶晶的，灰胡须硬邦邦的，尾巴像一长截黑橡胶。池塘里游着一群小鸭，活像一窝黄灿灿的金丝雀。鸭妈妈浑身雪白，长着货真价实的红腿，正教孩子们在水里倒立。
“要是不会倒立，你们永远进不了上流社会。”她反复叮咛，隔一会儿便亲自做给他们看。小鸭们却根本不理她。他们那么小，还不知道进了那个社会到底有什么好处。
“多不听话的孩子！”老水鼠叫道，“真该把他们淹死。”
“才不呢，”鸭妈妈回答，“谁都有初学的时候。做父母的，再耐心些也不为过。”
“啊，父母的心情我是一点也不懂，”水鼠说，“我又没有家室。说实话，我从没结过婚，以后也不打算结。爱情自有它的好处，可友情比它高尚多了。要我说，世上最高贵、最难得的，莫过于忠贞不渝的友谊。”
“那么请教您，您觉得一个忠实的朋友该尽些什么义务？”附近柳树上有一只绿雀，恰好听到他们谈话，便开口问。
“对呀，我也正想知道。”鸭妈妈说着，游到池塘另一头倒立起来，给孩子们做个好榜样。
“问得真傻！”水鼠叫道，“我当然指望我忠实的朋友对我忠实啦。”
“那您怎样回报他呢？”小鸟在一枝银色的柳条上荡着，扇了扇小翅膀。
“我不明白你在说什么。”水鼠答道。
“说到这个，我给您讲个故事吧。”绿雀说。
“这个故事讲的是我吗？”水鼠问，“要是讲我，我就听。我可爱听虚构的故事了。”
“用在您身上也合适。”绿雀回答。他飞下树，在岸边落脚，给水鼠讲起《忠实的朋友》。
“从前，”绿雀说，“有一个老实的小伙子，名叫汉斯。”
“他很出众吗？”水鼠问。

“不，”绿雀答道，“除了那副和善的心肠，那张圆圆的、有趣的、总带着笑的脸，我想他算不上出众。他一个人住一所小屋，每天在花园里干活。方圆一带再没有比他那儿更好看的花园了。园子里有须苞石竹、紫罗兰花、荠菜和白花毛茛。有大马士革玫瑰和黄玫瑰，有淡紫的番红花，也有金黄的，有紫色和白色的堇菜。还有耧斗菜、草地碎米荠、马郁兰、野罗勒、黄花九轮草、鸢尾、黄水仙和香石竹。月份往前走，它们就依次抽苞、绽放，一种花接了另一种花的位置，总有美丽的东西可看，总有芬芳的香气可闻。
“小汉斯有好多朋友，最忠实的一个要数大个子磨坊主休。这个富有的磨坊主对他实在是忠实。每次经过汉斯的花园，他总要探过墙头，采一大捧花，或是抓一把香草。赶上果子熟了，就往两个口袋里装满李子和樱桃。
“‘真正的朋友，就得什么东西都一同分享。’磨坊主常常这么说。小汉斯就点头微笑，为自己有个想法如此高尚的朋友而骄傲。
“有时候，邻居们倒觉得奇怪。富有的磨坊主明明囤着一百袋面粉，养着六头奶牛，还有好大一群长着厚羊毛的羊，怎么从来没拿什么东西回赠小汉斯？汉斯自己可从不为这些事伤脑筋。能听磨坊主讲那些真挚友情如何无私的妙论，他别提多高兴了。
“小汉斯就这样埋头侍弄他的花园。春天、夏天、秋天，他快快乐乐。到了冬天，既没有果子也没有花可拿去上市，他就得挨饿受冻，晚饭常常只有几片干梨或几颗硬果仁，吃完便只好上床。冬天他也很寂寞，因为这时磨坊主从来不上门看他。
“‘只要积雪还在，我去看小汉斯有什么益处？’磨坊主常对妻子说，‘人落难时就该让他一个人静静，别去打扰。至少，我对友情是这么想的，我敢肯定我没错。所以我要等到春天再去拜访他。到时候，他就能给我一大篮报春花，心里该有多快活！’
“‘你待人可真周到，’妻子坐在扶手椅里，靠着烧得旺旺的松木柴火，舒服地回答，‘真是周到呀。听你讲友情是一种享受。就连牧师大人也说不出你这样漂亮的话吧，虽说他住着三层楼的房子，小手指还戴着金戒指。’
“‘那为什么不请小汉斯到咱们这里来呢？’磨坊主的小儿子问，‘要是可怜的汉斯正遇到难处，我愿意分他半碗粥，还领他去看我的小白兔。’

“‘你这孩子真傻！’磨坊主叫道，‘我真不知道送你上学有什么用，你好像什么也没学会。想想看，小汉斯上我们这儿来，一看我们烤着暖炉，吃着好饭，还有一大桶红葡萄酒，说不定会起嫉妒心。嫉妒多可怕，什么人的天性都能叫它毁掉。我当然不能让汉斯的天性遭到破坏。我是他最好的朋友，要一直照看他，免得他受到诱惑。何况，汉斯要是来了，说不定想从我这里赊点面粉，这我可做不到。面粉是一回事，友情是另一回事，两样不能混淆。你瞧，这两个词连拼法都不一样，意思更是截然不同，谁都看得出来。’
“‘你可真会说话！’磨坊主太太给自己倒了满满一杯温啤酒，‘我听得都犯困了，简直像坐在教堂里一样。’
“‘会做好事的人多了，’磨坊主回答，‘可话能说得漂亮的人少极了。这就说明两者之中，说要比做难得多，也高明得多。’他隔着桌子严厉地望了小儿子一眼。儿子惭愧得低下头，涨得满脸通红，泪珠滴进茶杯里。好在他还这么小，你们就原谅他吧。”
“故事完了？”水鼠问。
“当然没有，”绿雀答道，“这才是开头。”
“那你可真落伍了，”水鼠说，“如今凡是会讲故事的人，都是结尾先讲，再讲开头，最后用中间收尾。这叫新方法。前几天，一位评论家陪一个年轻人绕池塘散步，我亲耳听他说起过，谈得可详尽了。我敢断定他说得对。他戴着蓝眼镜，是个光头，每回那年轻人开口议论，他总回答一声‘呸！’不过请你接着讲吧。我真喜欢那位磨坊主。我自己也有各种高尚的情操，可见我跟他实在投缘。”
“好吧，”绿雀一会儿用这条腿跳跳，一会儿换那条腿跳跳，“冬天刚刚过去，报春花开始张开淡黄色的小星星，磨坊主便对妻子说要下山去看小汉斯。
“‘哎哟，你的心肠多好！’妻子叫道，‘你总是惦记别人。可别忘了带上大篮子装花。’
“磨坊主便用一条结实的铁链拴牢风车的叶片，臂弯里挎着篮子下了山。
“‘早啊，小汉斯。’磨坊主说。
“‘早啊。’汉斯拄着铁锹回答，笑得嘴快咧到了耳根。
“‘这个冬天你过得怎么样？’磨坊主问。
“‘啊，谢谢你问起我，’汉斯喊道，‘你真好，真的。日子只怕算是相当难过，不过眼下春天来了，我高兴得很，满园的花都长得好。’
“‘冬天里我们常提到你呢，汉斯，’磨坊主说，‘总想着你日子过得怎么样。’
“‘你们真好，’汉斯说，‘我还有点担心你把我忘了呢。’
“‘汉斯，你叫我很吃惊，’磨坊主说，‘友情从来不会遗忘。这正是它的妙处。不过你恐怕不懂得生活的诗意。话说回来，你的报春花开得多漂亮！’
“‘确实漂亮，’汉斯说，‘幸好我有这么多。我正要送到集市上，卖给镇长的女儿，再拿那笔钱把我的独轮车买回来。’
“‘把独轮车买回来？你该不是把它给卖了吧？这事办得多傻！’
“‘事情是这样的，’汉斯说，‘我也是没办法。你知道，我整个冬天过得很苦，实在没有钱买面包。我先卖掉了礼拜天穿的外套上的银扣子，再卖掉银链，然后卖掉大烟斗，最后卖掉了独轮车。不过如今我正要一件件把它们买回来。’
“‘汉斯，’磨坊主说，‘我把我的独轮车送给你。它不算很完好，一边的车板掉了，车轮辐条也出了点毛病。尽管如此，我还是肯送给你。我知道我这样做很慷慨，许多人会觉得我就这么舍了它，傻得不得了，可我不随大流。我看，慷慨就是友情的精髓。再说，我自己已经有一辆新独轮车了。对，你只管放心，我会把我的独轮车送给你。’
“‘呀，你真大方。’小汉斯说，快活得那张有趣的圆脸整个亮了起来，‘我很容易就能把它修好，我家里有块木板。’
“‘一块木板！’磨坊主说，‘哎呀，我正缺这个修谷仓的屋顶呢。上面破了好大一个洞，不补上，谷子统统要受潮。幸好你提起来了！多奇妙，一桩好事总能引出另一桩来。我给了你独轮车，现在你又要把木板送我。当然，独轮车可比这块木板值钱多了，可真正的友情从不计较这些。请你马上去拿，我今天就要动手修谷仓。’
“‘当然行。’小汉斯叫道，跑到棚里，把木板拖了出来。
“‘木板可不大啊，’磨坊主瞧了瞧说，‘恐怕等我修完谷仓屋顶就剩不下什么给你补车子了。这当然不能怪我。还有，既然我把独轮车都给你了，你准愿意回送我几朵花。篮子在这里，可要装得满满的。’
“‘装得满满的？’小汉斯说，心里有点难过。那篮子实在大得很，他知道，一旦装满就不会剩下什么花可以拿上市集，而他实在很想买回他的银扣子。
“‘说真的，’磨坊主回答，‘既然我把独轮车都给了你，朝你要几朵花想来也不算过分。也许我错了，可我一向以为，友情，真正的友情，决没有哪怕一丝一毫的自私。’
“‘亲爱的朋友，我最好的朋友！’小汉斯喊道，‘你喜欢我园子里什么花，尽管拿！只要你能看得起我，什么时候都比拿回银扣子要紧。’他一溜跑去，摘下所有美丽的报春花，把磨坊主的篮子装得满满的。
“‘再见，小汉斯。’磨坊主扛着木板，手提大篮子，上山去了。
“‘再见。’小汉斯说。他又快快乐乐地挖起地来，一想到独轮车，他就觉得满心欢喜。
“第二天，他正把金银花的藤钉在门廊上，忽然听见磨坊主在路上唤他。他跳下梯子，跑过花园，从墙头往外张望。
“磨坊主就在外面，背着一大袋面粉。
“‘亲爱的小汉斯，’磨坊主说，‘能麻烦你替我把这袋面粉扛到集市上去吗？’
“‘哎呀，真过意不去，’汉斯说，‘可我今天实在很忙。所有这些藤蔓都得钉上去，花都等着浇，草地也全得用滚筒压一遍。’
“‘说真的，’磨坊主说，‘想想我就要把独轮车送给你，你这么拒绝，好像不太像朋友吧。’
“‘哎，可别这么说，’小汉斯喊道，‘哪怕你拿整个世界换，我也不肯做个不够朋友的人。’他跑回去拿帽子，背起大面袋，吃力地上路了。
“那天很热，路上灰尘扑面，还没到第六块里程碑，汉斯就累得非坐下歇歇不可。他依旧鼓起勇气往前走，总算到了集市。在那里等了一阵，他以相当不错的价钱卖掉了这袋面粉，随即赶回家去，生怕耽搁太晚，会在路上撞见强盗。
“‘今天着实够辛苦的，’小汉斯睡前对自己说，‘好在我没拒绝磨坊主。他是我最好的朋友，何况他还要把独轮车送给我呢。’
“第二天一早，磨坊主下山来取卖面粉的钱。小汉斯实在累坏了，还躺在床上。

“‘我说，你可真懒，’磨坊主说，‘说真的，既然我打算把独轮车给你，我看你可以更勤快一点。懒惰是大罪过，我的朋友里若有谁懈怠偷懒，我可不喜欢。我说话直，你不要见怪。当然，倘若我不是你朋友，做梦也不会这样说。但朋友之间要是不能有话直说，做朋友还有什么用？拣漂亮话说，哄人家高兴，拍人家的马屁，谁都会。真正的朋友总是专挑不中听的话讲，也不怕刺痛人。说实在的，要是真朋友，他巴不得这样，因为他知道这么做是在行善。’
“‘真不好意思，’小汉斯揉着眼，摘下睡帽，‘我实在太累了，就想在床上躺一会儿，听听鸟唱歌。你知不知道，我听过鸟唱歌，干起活来总是更带劲？’
“‘那我可高兴了，’磨坊主拍拍小汉斯的背，‘因为我正要你一穿好衣服就上磨坊来，替我修谷仓屋顶呢。’
“可怜的小汉斯一心想去花园干活。他的花已经两天没浇水了。可磨坊主是他那么要好的朋友，他怎么好意思推辞呢。
“‘要是我说手头正忙，你会觉得我不够朋友吗？’他羞怯胆小地问。
“‘这么说吧，’磨坊主回答，‘想想我就要把独轮车送给你，我觉得这点要求谈不上太高。当然啦，你若拒绝，我就自己去做。’
“‘哎呀！那绝对使不得。’小汉斯嚷起来。他跳下床穿好衣服，上谷仓去了。
“他在那儿忙了一整天，一直忙到日落。太阳落山时，磨坊主才来看看他做得如何。
“‘小汉斯，屋顶上的洞补好了没有？’磨坊主欢欢喜喜地叫道。
“‘全补好了。’小汉斯回答着，从梯子上下来。
“‘啊！’磨坊主说，‘世上再没有比替别人干活更叫人快乐的事了。’
“‘能听你讲话，真是我的福气，’小汉斯坐下来，抹了抹额头，‘天大的福气。不过我恐怕永远不会有你那么美好的想法。’
“‘噢，你会有的，’磨坊主说，‘不过还得多花点工夫。目前你对友情只有实践，将来有一天你也能掌握理论。’
“‘你真觉得我能行吗？’小汉斯问。
“‘我毫不怀疑，’磨坊主回答，‘不过现在屋顶修好了，你最好回去休息，明天我还要你帮我把羊赶到山上去。’
“可怜的小汉斯不敢说什么。第二天清早，磨坊主把羊群赶到他的小屋旁，汉斯便带着羊往山里走。这一来一回用了他整整一天。回家时他疲倦极了，坐在椅子上就睡着，一直到大天亮才醒来。
“‘今天在花园里，我准能过得很快活。’他说完，立刻就着手干活。
“可不知怎的，他总是照管不到自己的花。他的磨坊主朋友老是跑来，打发他跑好远的路办事，或是叫他到磨坊帮忙。有时小汉斯很难过，担心花儿会以为自己忘了它们。他只好想着磨坊主是自己最好的朋友，拿这念头安慰自己。‘再说，’他常常说，‘他还要送我独轮车，这完全出于慷慨。’
“小汉斯就这样忙着替磨坊主干活。磨坊主呢，讲了种种关于友情的漂亮话。汉斯用一本笔记簿记下来，夜里常常反复诵读。他实在是个好学生。
“有天晚上，小汉斯坐在自家炉火旁，忽然有人重重敲门。那晚风雨肆虐，风绕着屋子怒吼，起先他还当是风暴闹出的声音。但很快又敲了一下，接着是第三下，比前两下都响。
“‘准是个可怜的过路人。’小汉斯对自己说，一溜跑去开门。
“站在门口的是磨坊主。他一手提灯，一手拄着粗棍子。
“‘亲爱的小汉斯，’磨坊主叫道，‘我遇上大麻烦了。我的小儿子从梯子上摔下来，受了伤。我本打算去找医生，可他住得那么远，今晚天气又这么坏，我刚刚想到，让你替我去要好得多。你知道我就要把独轮车送给你。那么，你为我做点事当作回报，也是应该的。’
“‘当然，’小汉斯叫道，‘你肯来找我，是看得起我。我马上动身。可你得把灯借给我，夜里这么黑，我怕会掉进沟里。’
“‘真过意不去，’磨坊主答道，‘可这是我的新灯，它要是出了点什么事，我的损失可就大了。’
“‘那没关系，没有灯我也去！’小汉斯说。他取下厚皮大衣和暖和的鲜红帽子，把围巾系在脖子上，出发了。
“那是多可怕的一场风暴！夜色黑得小汉斯几乎看不见，风刮得他几乎站不稳。可他非常勇敢，大约走了三个钟头，终于来到医生家门前，抬手敲门。
“‘外头是谁？’医生把头探出卧室窗子问。
“‘是小汉斯，医生。’
“‘有什么事，小汉斯？’
“‘磨坊主的儿子从梯子上摔下来，受了伤。磨坊主请你马上过去。’
“‘好！’医生叫人备马，拿来长靴和提灯，随即下楼，骑马朝磨坊主家奔去。小汉斯吃力地跟在后头。
“可是风暴愈来愈凶，雨像从天上倒下来。小汉斯既看不清自己往哪里走，又赶不上马。最后他迷了路，不知不觉走进荒野。那里到处是深坑，非常危险。可怜的小汉斯就在那里淹死了。第二天，几个放山羊的人发现他的身体浮在一大汪水里，便把他送回了小屋。
“小汉斯太招人喜欢了，大家都去参加他的葬礼。磨坊主成了头一号哀悼的人。
“‘我是他最好的朋友，’磨坊主说，‘理应给我最好的位置。’他便披着黑色长斗篷，走在送葬队伍的最前头，不时掏出一块大手帕擦擦眼睛。
“‘小汉斯一走，大家的损失可真大。’葬礼结束后，大伙儿安舒服服坐在客栈里，喝着香料酒，吃着甜糕点，铁匠这样说。
“‘至少我的损失是很大的，’磨坊主回答，‘嗐，我那辆独轮车都算是送给他了，现在可真不知道拿它怎么办。在家里，它摆在哪儿都碍着我的事。车又破成那个德性，想卖也卖不出什么钱。我以后可得留神，再也不送什么东西给人了。人太慷慨，总归要吃亏。’”
过了好一会儿，水鼠才说：“后来呢？”
“这个嘛，这就是结尾。”绿雀说。
“可那位磨坊主后来怎么样了？”水鼠问。
“哦，那我真不知道，”绿雀答道，“我也的确不关心。”
“看来你天生缺少同情心，这很明显。”水鼠说。
“我担心您还没领会这个故事的寓意。”绿雀说。
“领会什么？”水鼠尖声叫道。
“寓意。”
“你是说，这个故事里还有个寓意？”
“当然。”绿雀说。
“岂有此理，”水鼠气呼呼地说，“我看你开讲以前就该告诉我。你要是早说，我断然不会听。我会像那位评论家一样说‘呸！’不过我现在说也还来得及。”于是他用最大的嗓门嚷了声“呸”，尾巴一甩，回洞里去了。
“您觉得水鼠怎么样？”几分钟后，鸭妈妈划着水上前问，“他有好些优点哩。不过我有一颗做母亲的心，每次见到那种打定主意终身不娶的人，我总免不了热泪盈眶。”
“我担心自己惹恼了他，”绿雀答道，“事情是这样，我给他讲了个有寓意的故事。”
“唉！这可一向是件非常危险的事。”鸭妈妈说。
这一点，我和她的看法完全一致。

source_paragraphs: THE King’s son was going to be married, so there were general rejoicings. He had waited a whole year for his bride, and at last she had arrived.
